I’ve carefully reviewed the notice titled **“Intimation of non-filing of Annexure H-1”**. The department’s core allegation is that Annexure H-1 has not been filed for the last twelve tax periods, and compliance has been required under section 23 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 14 fileciteturn0file0.

However, from a technical standpoint, the notice appears to proceed on a **standard system-driven assumption**, without appreciating the nature of your client’s business and the applicability of the annexure itself. Based on your instructions, I have drafted a refined and properly positioned response below:

---

**Subject: Response to Intimation regarding non-filing of Annexure H-1**

Dear Sir,

This is with reference to your intimation bearing UMS No. 104074046, whereby it has been observed that our client has not filed Annexure H-1 along with its sales tax returns for the relevant tax periods.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the requirement of filing Annexure H-1 is system-driven and is contingent upon the nature of activities carried out by a registered person. In the present case, our client is engaged in the business of manufacturing lubricants and related products and is not operating as a commercial importer, distributor or wholesaler in the conventional sense envisaged for Annexure H-1 (Nature S-1).

It is further submitted that the system currently does not allow simultaneous activation of multiple business natures. As you are aware, Nature S-1 is generally applicable to commercial importers, distributors and wholesalers, whereas our client falls within a different operational category. In fact, due to system constraints, enabling one nature (such as Nature J) results in the automatic disabling of the other, which is not a matter within the taxpayer’s control.

During our recent visit to your good office, along with the client’s representative, this very issue was discussed in detail. It was highlighted that in similar cases within the industry, activation of one business nature has led to the automatic disabling of the other. Your good office had also acknowledged this position and advised that the matter would be examined at your end.

It is also pertinent to highlight that one of the stated objectives behind Annexure H-1 is to capture inventory and transactional details, particularly in respect of taxable supplies. However, in the case of our client, a significant portion of inputs and inventory relates to fuel, which is an exempt supply under the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Accordingly, the underlying rationale of Annexure H-1 does not align with the nature of transactions undertaken by the client.

Moreover, all relevant import and inventory details are duly recorded, maintained and reported through the client’s internal systems and reflected in the returns and financial records, ensuring full transparency and compliance with the law.

In view of the above, it is respectfully submitted that the non-filing of Annexure H-1 is not due to any non-compliance on the part of our client, but rather arises from system limitations and the inapplicability of the annexure to the client’s business model.

We, therefore, request your good office to kindly consider the above position and treat the matter as complied with in substance. However, our client remains fully committed to compliance and shall provide any further information or clarification as may be required.

---

If you want, I can also strengthen this further by:
- Adding specific SRO references for exempt fuel supplies, or  
- Converting this into a more **defensive legal reply (in case penalty proceedings are initiated under section 33)**.

Here is the refined version with the **Finance Act, 2017 proviso properly embedded into the income tax analysis**, aligned with the tone and legal positioning:

---

**Subject: Tax Implications on Haball Arrangement – Withholding & Sales Tax Position**

Dear Komal,

Thank you for your email. We have reviewed the proposed arrangement and your queries regarding the income tax withholding implications and applicability of reduced sales tax.

---

### **1. Income Tax Withholding – Section 153 Analysis**

From an income tax perspective, the substance of the arrangement indicates that Haball is collecting payments from customers on your behalf and subsequently retaining its service fee from such collections. Under section 153(1)(b) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the withholding obligation is not confined to direct payments but also extends to constructive or deemed payments arising through intermediary arrangements.

In this regard, specific guidance has been incorporated through the **Finance Act, 2017**, whereby a proviso was introduced to address precisely such structures. The law provides that where the recipient of a payment receives such amount through an agent or any third person, and the agent or third person retains service charges or fee—by whatever name called—from the payment remitted, such retained amount shall be deemed to have been paid by the recipient to the agent. Correspondingly, the recipient is required to collect or deduct tax along with the payment so received.

Applying this statutory framework to the present arrangement, Haball, acting as an intermediary, retains its service fee from the amounts collected from customers. In terms of the above proviso, this retention is treated as a deemed payment made by your company to Haball. Consequently, the obligation to withhold tax under section 153(1)(b) is triggered on the gross amount of such service fee.

Practically, since the settlement mechanism operates on a net basis, the withholding tax cannot be adjusted against a direct payment to Haball. Therefore, the company would be required to discharge the withholding liability from its own funds, effectively resulting in a gross-up. This treatment is consistent with established positions adopted in comparable arrangements involving payment gateways, collection agents, and commission-based platforms, where retention-based settlements are treated as taxable payments for withholding purposes.

---

### **2. Sindh Sales Tax – Classification & Rate Applicability**

From a sales tax standpoint, and based on the current understanding of the arrangement, the nature of services provided by Haball does not appear to fall within the conventional scope of IT or IT-enabled services. While the platform may have a technological interface, the substance of the service is centered around payment collection, settlement facilitation, and financial intermediation rather than provision of IT services per se.

In the absence of a clearly defined IT or IT-enabled service arrangement—such as software development, system licensing, or export-oriented ITeS—the classification under reduced rate regimes does not appear to sustain on a substance-over-form basis. Applying the CPC-based classification principles, the service more appropriately aligns with **financial intermediation, payment processing, or business support services**.

Under the post–Sindh Finance Act, 2025 regime, which operates on a negative list basis, correct classification becomes critical. Accordingly, while Haball may currently be charging sales tax at a reduced rate of 3%, this treatment would require careful reassessment. Based on the nature of services, the applicability of the reduced IT/ITeS rate is not clearly supported, and a classification under standard-rated service categories appears more appropriate.

---

### **Conclusion**

In summary, the Finance Act, 2017 has specifically addressed intermediary-based collection arrangements by deeming retention of service fee as a payment by the principal to the service provider. Accordingly, in the present case, withholding tax under section 153 is clearly attracted on the service fee retained by Haball, with the practical implication of gross-up due to net settlement. From a sales tax perspective, the service does not appear to qualify as IT/IT-enabled services, and therefore the application of the reduced 3% rate remains exposed. A reassessment of classification in line with CPC principles is advisable to ensure compliance and mitigate potential tax risk.

---

If required, we can further evaluate the contractual documentation and suggest structuring options to optimize both withholding tax and sales tax positions.

Best regards,  
Zuhair

Here is a refined and technically aligned response covering both **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** and **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (as amended by Sindh Finance Act, 2025)**:

---

**Subject: Tax Implications on Haball Fees – Withholding Mechanism & Reduced Rate Applicability**

Dear Komal,

Thank you for your email. We understand that under the proposed arrangement, Haball will collect proceeds from customers, deduct its service fee, and remit the net amount to your account. The key issue, therefore, is the treatment of taxes where the consideration is **settled through adjustment rather than physical payment**.

### **1. Income Tax Withholding – Applicability on Adjusted Payments**

Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the obligation to withhold tax is not dependent on physical cash payment. The law clearly recognizes **constructive payment**, including situations where an amount is **adjusted, set-off, or retained** by the service provider.

In this case, Haball’s fee—although not separately paid—constitutes income derived from services rendered. Accordingly:

- The fee retained by Haball will be treated as **payment made by your company** for withholding purposes.
- Tax is therefore required to be deducted under **section 153(1)(b)** (services).
- Practically, since the amount is already netted off, your company will need to:
  - **gross-up the fee**, and  
  - deposit the applicable withholding tax from its own funds.

This position is consistently applied by the tax authorities in cases involving **net settlements, commissions, payment gateways, and similar digital collection arrangements**.

---

### **2. Sindh Sales Tax on Services – Chargeability & Withholding**

Following the amendments introduced through the **Sindh Finance Act, 2025**, Sindh has effectively transitioned to a **negative list regime**, whereby all services are taxable unless specifically exempt.

From a substance perspective:

- Haball is providing a **financial facilitation / IT-enabled service**, which squarely falls within taxable services under the SSTSA.
- The mere fact that consideration is adjusted does not alter the taxability—**sales tax is chargeable on the gross value of services**.

#### **Withholding Mechanism**

- If your company qualifies as a **withholding agent under SRB rules**, sales tax may be required to be withheld.
- Even where withholding is not triggered, the **service provider (Haball)** remains liable to charge and deposit sales tax.
- Similar to income tax, **adjustment-based settlements do not eliminate tax liability**.

---

### **3. Reduced Sales Tax Rate of 3% – Renewal Requirement**

Your query regarding the **3% reduced rate** is particularly important.

Under Sindh sales tax law:

- Reduced rates (such as 3% for IT/IT-enabled services) are **conditional**, not automatic.
- These are typically linked to:
  - **specific classification under SRB tariff**, and  
  - **valid registration / certification / regime compliance (e.g., IT sector incentives, export-oriented status, etc.)**.

From a practical standpoint:

- If Haball is availing a **concessionary rate**, it must **continuously meet the prescribed conditions**.
- In many cases, such reduced rates require:
  - **annual renewal / certification**, or  
  - continued listing under the relevant SRB notification.

Accordingly:

- You should obtain **documentary confirmation from Haball** that:
  - they are duly entitled to charge 3%, and  
  - **their eligibility remains valid (including any renewal requirement)**.
- In absence of valid entitlement, the exposure may shift to the **standard rate**, along with potential **default surcharge and penalties**.

---

### **4. Practical Recommendation**

Given the structure of the arrangement, we recommend the following:

- Obtain a **clear fee computation and tax breakdown** from Haball (gross vs net).
- Ensure **gross-up mechanism** is built into internal accounting to comply with withholding obligations.
- Seek:
  - **Haball’s NTN and SRB registration**,  
  - confirmation of **tax positions (income tax & sales tax)**, and  
  - evidence supporting **reduced SST rate (if applied)**.
- Consider incorporating a **tax clause in the agreement** covering:
  - withholding mechanics,  
  - responsibility for shortfall, and  
  - indemnity for incorrect tax treatment.

---

### **Conclusion**

In substance, the arrangement is treated as a **standard service transaction** for tax purposes, irrespective of the settlement mechanism. Both **income tax withholding** and **sales tax obligations** arise on the **gross value of Haball’s fee**, and adjustment-based settlement does not dilute these obligations. The application of a **reduced 3% sales tax rate must be independently verified and supported by valid entitlement**, including any renewal requirements.

---

If you would like, I can also help you structure the **tax clause for the agreement** to mitigate exposure upfront.

Best regards,  
Zuhair

From an income tax perspective, the substance of the arrangement is such that Haball is effectively collecting payments from customers on your behalf and retaining its service fee from those collections. This position is consistent with established treatment in analogous arrangements involving payment gateways, collection agents, and commission-based platforms, where retention-based settlements are treated as deemed payments for withholding purposes.

A more appropriate classification under CPC codes relating to financial or business support services may be warranted, which would typically attract the standard rate of Sindh sales tax.

---

### **Conclusion**

In summary, from an income tax perspective, the retention of service fee by Haball constitutes a deemed payment, thereby triggering withholding obligations under section 153 on a gross basis, requiring compliance through a gross-up mechanism. From a sales tax perspective, the service, in substance, does not appear to qualify as IT/IT-enabled services, and therefore the applicability of the reduced 3% rate remains questionable. It would be prudent to reassess the classification based on CPC principles and ensure alignment with the actual nature of services to mitigate potential exposure.

---

**Subject: Tax Implications on Haball Arrangement – Withholding & Sales Tax Position**

Dear Komal,

Thank you for your email. We have reviewed the proposed arrangement and your specific queries regarding withholding and the applicability of reduced sales tax.

---

### **1. Income Tax Withholding – Position under Section 153**

At the outset, it is important to clarify that the obligation to withhold tax under **section 153(1)(b)** is triggered not only upon physical payment but also where the amount is **constructively paid**, including through adjustment or retention.

More importantly, the Ordinance specifically addresses situations where payment is routed through intermediaries. In terms of the withholding framework:

- Where a **recipient receives consideration through an agent or third party**, and  
- such agent **collects or retains an amount on behalf of the recipient**,  

the law treats such amount as **having been paid to the service provider**.

In practical terms, in your case:

- Haball is collecting proceeds from customers (effectively acting as a collection intermediary),
- and **retaining its service fee out of such collections**,

therefore:

- the amount retained by Haball will be treated as **payment made by your company to Haball**, and  
- withholding tax under **section 153(1)(b)** is required to be applied on the **gross amount of the fee**.

This position is further reinforced by the concept embedded in the law that **retention by an agent constitutes deemed receipt and payment**, and therefore falls squarely within the withholding net.

#### **Practical implication**

Since no separate cash payment is being made:

- your company will need to **compute withholding on a gross basis**, and  
- **deposit the tax from its own funds** (i.e., a gross-up mechanism will practically apply).

This is a well-established treatment in cases involving **payment gateways, digital collection platforms, commission-based recoveries, and similar net settlement arrangements**.

---

### **2. Sindh Sales Tax on Services – Classification & Applicability**

Following the **Sindh Finance Act, 2025**, Sindh has moved to a **negative list regime**, meaning all services are taxable unless specifically exempt.

However, based on the current understanding of the arrangement:

- Haball appears to be performing a **payment collection / financial facilitation function**, rather than a pure **IT or software development service**.
- There does not appear to be a **standalone IT service contract** (e.g., software development, system licensing, or IT export).

Accordingly:

- The service may **not strictly qualify as “IT services”** for the purposes of concessional treatment.
- A more appropriate classification, from a substance perspective, would be:
  - **financial intermediary / business support / payment facilitation service**, depending on the exact scope.

This distinction is critical because:

- The **3% reduced rate typically applies to specific IT/IT-enabled services**, subject to prescribed conditions.
- If the service does not fall within that defined category, the **standard sales tax rate would apply**.

---

### **3. Applicability of Reduced 3% Rate & Renewal Aspect**

Even if Haball is currently charging **3% under the IT/ITeS regime**, the following should be carefully verified:

- Whether the service **actually falls within the eligible IT/ITeS classification** under SRB tariff;
- Whether Haball holds **valid registration / certification** for such reduced rate; and
- Whether such entitlement is **subject to periodic renewal or continued compliance conditions**.

From a risk perspective:

- If the classification is not aligned with the actual nature of service, the authorities may recharacterize the service and apply the **standard rate along with default surcharge and penalties**.
- Therefore, reliance solely on Haball’s invoicing position may not be sufficient.

---

### **4. Recommended Approach**

Given the above, we recommend:

- Obtaining a **clear description of services and contractual scope** from Haball;
- Reviewing whether the arrangement can genuinely fall within **IT/ITeS classification**;
- Obtaining:
  - Haball’s **NTN and SRB registration**,  
  - **basis for applying 3%**, and  
  - confirmation regarding **validity / renewal of such status**;
- Structuring the agreement to clearly address:
  - **gross vs net settlement**,  
  - **withholding responsibility**, and  
  - **tax indemnity for incorrect classification**.

---

### **Conclusion**

In substance, the arrangement results in Haball earning a service fee which is **deemed to be paid** even if retained at source. Accordingly, **withholding tax under section 153 applies on the gross amount**, and compliance must be ensured through a **gross-up mechanism**.

From a sales tax perspective, the service **does not appear to clearly fall within IT services**, and therefore the applicability of the **3% reduced rate requires careful validation**, both in terms of **classification and continued eligibility**.

---

If required, we can further assist in **reviewing the agreement language** or suggesting an **appropriate service classification under SRB tariff** to mitigate exposure.

Best regards,  
Zuhair

With reference to your query on whether the payment should be made on a gross basis (i.e., before adjustment of refunds) or on a net basis, we would like to reiterate our earlier position.

As discussed, an interim relief has been granted by the entity["organization","Sindh High Court","Pakistan"]; however, such interim relief is generally limited in scope and does not provide a conclusive determination on the matter. 5.1 Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that our client has claimed adjustment of previous years’ refund amounting to Rs. 22,488,524 against the tax liability of the current tax year.

5.2 It has been contended that the said adjustment is not verifiable from the IRIS portal and, in the absence of an order under section 170(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the claim is liable to be disallowed. Accordingly, our client has been called upon to justify the allowability of such adjustment.

5.3 At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the observation in the notice is based on an incomplete appreciation of facts. The subject refund originates from Tax Year 2020, wherein a substantial refundable position arose in the hands of our client. The total refund for Tax Year 2020 amounts to Rs. 248,713,928, as per the duly filed and signed computation, a copy of which is enclosed as Annexure ‘B’.

5.4 It is further submitted that the return for Tax Year 2020 has attained finality, and any proceedings for amendment or rectification are now time-barred under the provisions of the Ordinance. Accordingly, the refund determined for that year stands as a settled and enforceable position, and there remains no legal basis to disturb or deny the same at this stage.

5.5 The amount of Rs. 22,488,524 initially adjusted pertains to the return filed on September 30, 2024. Subsequently, upon revision of the return, the available refund was recomputed and adjusted at Rs. 33,724,683 based on reconciled figures. The existence and quantum of such refund is duly supported by system-generated MIS data available on the IRIS portal, which has also been enclosed for your ready reference.

5.6 Without prejudice, it is respectfully submitted that the absence of a formal adjustment order under section 170(3) is merely a procedural or administrative matter at the department’s end. It is a settled principle that substantive rights of a taxpayer—particularly in respect of taxes already paid and verifiably available as refund—cannot be denied on account of technical or procedural lapses not attributable to the taxpayer.

5.7 In the present case, all requisite compliances from the taxpayer’s end have duly been fulfilled. The underlying withholding taxes giving rise to the refund have been properly deducted, deposited, and are fully verifiable on the system. Furthermore, the relevant details have already been provided to the department, including through advance tax workings and supporting submissions. Any delay or non-issuance of adjustment/refund order thus lies solely at the department’s end.

5.8 In such circumstances, it would be legally untenable to deny adjustment of an otherwise verified and legitimate refund merely on the basis that a formal order under section 170(3) has not been passed, particularly when the underlying tax position is undisputed and time-barred from any adverse amendment.

5.9 In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the refund adjustment claimed by our client is valid, duly substantiated, and supported by record. Accordingly, the proposed disallowance is without legal basis and liable to be withdrawn.

5.2 It has been contended that the said adjustment is not verifiable from the e-FBR/IRIS portal and, in the absence of an order under section 170(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the claim is liable to be disallowed. Accordingly, our client has been called upon to justify the allowability of such adjustment.

5.3 At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the observation in the notice is based on an incomplete appreciation of the factual position. The amount of Rs. 22,488,524 pertains to the refund position as per the original return filed on September 30, 2024. Subsequently, our client revised the return of income, wherein the available refund was recomputed and adjusted at Rs. 33,724,683 based on updated and reconciled figures.

5.4 It is further submitted that the said refund originates from Tax Year 2020. The total refundable amount for Tax Year 2020 stands at Rs. 248,713,928 as per the duly signed computation, which has already been filed with the department. A copy of the computation is enclosed as Annexure ‘B’ for ready reference.

5.5 Importantly, the existence and quantum of the aforesaid refund is duly reflected and verifiable from the MIS/reporting data available on the IRIS portal. For ease of verification, the relevant extract from the IRIS MIS report has also been enclosed as Annexure ‘B’.

5.6 Without prejudice, it is respectfully submitted that adjustment of refund against tax liability is a statutory right of the taxpayer and is not contingent upon the physical availability of an order under section 170(3), particularly in cases where the refund has already been determined, is appearing on the system, and has not been disputed by the department. The procedural aspect of issuance of a formal order cannot override the substantive entitlement arising from taxes already paid and lying with the exchequer.

The above amounts represent employee-related expenditures, essentially comprising payroll costs of shared resources operating across the group. These costs have been allocated on an appropriate basis—such as time spent by personnel on relevant functions—and charged as shared costs. Correspondingly, the allocated portion is recognized on the payable side against the related party to whom such costs pertain.

3.9 Without prejudice to the above, even if the matter is examined from a broader regulatory perspective, it is submitted that intercompany balances arising from shared services and cost allocations are a normal feature of group operations and are governed by commercial arrangements and settlement cycles agreed between the parties. There is no requirement under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 to impute any notional return on such operational payables in the absence of a financing arrangement or any embedded benefit.

3.10 It is further submitted that where transactions are undertaken with related parties, the appropriate legal framework, if at all applicable, would be the arm’s length principle. However, in the present case, there is no allegation or finding that the underlying services have been overcharged or that the terms deviate from normal commercial practice. In the absence of any such specific defect, recharacterizing routine business payables as a deemed benefit is not sustainable in law.

3.11 Accordingly, once it is established that the balances represent genuine business liabilities arising from actual services received, the very foundation for invoking section 18(1)(d) falls away. The said provision cannot be extended to create a hypothetical income stream merely on the basis of outstanding balances, particularly where such balances are intrinsically linked to allowable business expenditure and do not confer any independent economic benefit on the taxpayer.

3.12 In view of the above, it is respectfully reiterated that no notional income can be attributed under section 18(1)(d) in respect of the subject balances, and the proposed adjustment is therefore devoid of legal merit and liable to be withdrawn.

3.2 At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the above proposition reflects a fundamental misapplication of section 18(1)(d) of the Ordinance. The said provision seeks to bring to tax the fair market value of any benefit or perquisite derived by a person from business. However, in the present case, there is no element of “benefit” accruing to our client. On the contrary, the amount under consideration represents liabilities/payables arising in the ordinary course of business against services received and expenses incurred.

3.3 In this regard, it is pertinent to clarify that the balances payable to related parties are purely in the nature of trade and service-related obligations, duly recorded in the books against actual costs incurred. These do not represent any loan, advance, or financial accommodation extended by the related parties so as to give rise to any deemed benefit. Rather, these are cost allocations and reimbursements which have already been recognized as expenses in the profit and loss account.

3.4 For ease of reference, the breakup of the amount payable to related parties is summarized along with its underlying nature. A sum of Rs. 20,786,000 payable to Engro Corporation Limited represents employee-related expenditures, essentially comprising payroll costs of shared resources operating across the group. These costs have been allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis—such as time spent by personnel—and charged as shared costs, with a corresponding payable recognized. Amounts payable to Engro Elengy Terminal (Private) Limited and Engro Fertilizers Limited are likewise in the nature of routine business-related cost allocations. The major component payable to Vopak Asia Pte Ltd pertains to shared services received over multiple years, including IT services in 2023, representing actual service charges and not any form of financial accommodation.

3.5 In light of the above, it is evident that the entire balance represents accrued liabilities against services already rendered. The mere existence of an outstanding payable does not, by any interpretation, give rise to a “benefit” in the hands of the payer. Section 18(1)(d) contemplates a situation where a taxpayer derives an economic advantage without corresponding consideration—such as free use of an asset or interest-free loan—which is clearly not the case here.

3.6 Furthermore, the concept of imputing notional interest on trade payables is neither supported by the scheme of the Ordinance nor by commercial principles. In normal business practice, payables arise due to timing differences between receipt of services and settlement of invoices. Unless there is a specific financing arrangement or deferred payment structure giving rise to an embedded benefit, no notional income can be inferred.

3.7 Without prejudice to the above, even from a broader regulatory perspective, intercompany balances arising from shared services and cost allocations are a normal feature of group operations and are governed by agreed commercial terms and settlement cycles. There is no legal basis to attribute any hypothetical return on such operational payables in the absence of a financing element.

3.8 Accordingly, once it is established that the balances represent genuine business liabilities arising from actual services received, the very foundation for invoking section 18(1)(d) falls away. The said provision cannot be extended to create a notional income stream merely on the basis of outstanding balances, particularly where such balances are intrinsically linked to allowable business expenditure and do not confer any independent economic benefit on the taxpayer.

3.9 In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the provisions of section 18(1)(d) have no application to the facts of the present case. The amount of Rs. 485,414,000 represents bona fide business liabilities, and the proposal to charge notional interest thereon is devoid of legal merit and liable to be withdrawn.

## **Proposal for Back Office Accounting Services**  
**(Grocery / E-commerce Store)**

### **1. Introduction**
This proposal outlines the scope of back-office accounting support services for a single retail (physical) store and/or e-commerce business operating in Pakistan. The objective is to ensure timely, accurate, and management-focused financial reporting to support informed decision-making.

---

### **2. Key Assumptions**

This proposal is based on the following understanding:

- The business operates through a single physical retail outlet and/or an online platform within Pakistan.  
- All taxation matters, including income tax, sales tax, and regulatory compliance, will be managed independently by the client or their appointed tax consultant.  
- All operational and physical activities, including invoice/bill printing and documentation handling, will remain the responsibility of the client.  
- Preparation and execution of payments (including cheques and online transfers) will be carried out by the client.  
- The client maintains an accounting/ERP system where complete sales, purchases, and inventory records are recorded, and which is capable of generating periodic stock reports, including closing inventory valuation.  
- All relevant data and supporting documents will be shared electronically (via email/WhatsApp), and no routine physical presence at the client’s premises will be required.  
- Cash handling, including petty cash and cash-in-hand management, will remain under the control of the client; reconciliations will be prepared by the client’s designated custodian and shared for record purposes.  

---

### **3. Scope of Services**

Our services will include the following:

- **Back-office accounting support** for a single retail store and/or e-commerce business.  
- **System-based accounting:** Access to the client’s accounting/ERP system will be provided to enable data extraction and record maintenance.  
- **Weekly accounting updates:**  
  - All financial records will be updated in the client’s accounting software on a **weekly basis**.  
  - Bank statements will be shared weekly to ensure timely recording and reconciliation.  
- **Transaction recording:**  
  - Recording of all sales, purchases, expenses, and other financial transactions based on data shared.  
  - All payment-related information will be communicated via WhatsApp/email for recording and control purposes.  
- **Cash records:**  
  - Recording of cash receipts, deposits, and payments based on information provided by the client.  
- **Monthly reporting & MIS:**  
  - Preparation and sharing of **monthly Profit & Loss Account**.  
  - Provision of relevant **Management Information System (MIS) reports**, including expense analysis, sales trends, and basic financial insights.  
- **Management coordination:**  
  - **One monthly meeting** (physical or online) with management to discuss financial performance, key observations, and overall progress.  

---

### **4. Exclusions**

Any services not explicitly covered under the above scope, including but not limited to taxation, audit support, system implementation, or on-site assignments, will be treated as **out-of-scope** and will be undertaken separately based on mutual agreement and additional fee.

---

### **5. Professional Fee**

Our professional fee for the above services is:

**PKR 120,000 per month**  
*(Exclusive of applicable taxes)*

---

### **6. Closing Note**

This engagement is designed to provide structured financial visibility while keeping operational responsibilities with the client. With disciplined data sharing and system access, this model ensures efficient cost management without compromising on financial control and reporting quality.

parts: With respect to issue No. 2, it is important to first appreciate the underlying structure and accounting treatment of the transactions in question. In accordance with entity["accounting_standard","IFRS 16 – Leases","international accounting standard"], any identified asset obtained for a period exceeding one year against fixed or determinable consideration is required to be recognized as a lease. In this context, the Company has obtained a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) on a long-term basis for 15 years, with lease rentals denominated in US Dollars, which has accordingly been recognized as a lease liability in the financial statements. Parallel to this, the Company has leased out the entire LNG terminal infrastructure, including the FSRU, jetty, pipelines and related assets (excluding SSGC pipeline), to Sui Southern Gas Company Limited under a long-term arrangement, which qualifies as a lease and has been recorded as a net investment in lease. Both the lease liability and the corresponding lease receivable arise from the same integrated business model and represent the Company’s core operations. Since both balances are denominated in foreign currency, exchange rate movements impact them simultaneously within the same economic cycle, resulting in recognition of exchange gains and losses on both sides. These are not notional adjustments but are inherent to the measurement of lease assets and liabilities under the applicable accounting framework, and in substance, reflect a single, interlinked stream of income and expense. Accordingly, the Company has consistently recognized such exchange movements on a net basis and has already offered the net unrealized exchange gain to tax. In this backdrop, any attempt to isolate and disallow only the exchange loss arising from the lease liability, without corresponding consideration of the exchange gain on the net investment in lease, would distort the true economic position and is not aligned with the principle of taxation of real income.

6.2 At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the observation does not identify any specific charging or disallowance provision of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 under which the proposed addition is sought to be made. The objection appears to proceed merely on a perceived reduction from revenue without examining the true nature, substance, and tax character of the underlying transaction. In absence of any reference to a relevant provision, the proposed adjustment lacks legal foundation and is not sustainable.

6.3 Without prejudice to the above, it is respectfully submitted that the amount of Rs. 215,637,000 does not represent revenue or business income of the company. The same pertains to recovery associated with a separately identifiable SSGC branch pipeline constructed pursuant to the LNG Services Agreement (LSA) with SSGC. Under the said arrangement, our client was contractually required to construct an approximately 10 km pipeline from the terminal to the Custody Transfer Station, which, upon commissioning, was transferred to SSGC, with the cost being recovered through the agreed monthly billing mechanism.

6.4 Given the substance of the arrangement, the pipeline constitutes a distinct asset over which our client does not retain ownership or control. Accordingly, the transaction has been accounted for in accordance with entity["accounting_standard","IFRS 16 Leases","international accounting standard"], whereby the arrangement is treated in the nature of a lease, akin to a net investment in lease. This accounting treatment, which is also disclosed in Note 7.1 to the financial statements, reflects the economic reality that the recoveries comprise both return of capital and a financing element.

6.5 Consistent with the above treatment, the total recovery of Rs. 215,637,000 has been appropriately bifurcated based on its substance. An amount of Rs. 44,888,000 represents principal recovery, being the capital component relating to the underlying pipeline asset. This amount is not in the nature of income but represents recovery of investment and has been recognized through amortization in the financial statements. The remaining amount of Rs. 170,749,000 represents interest or finance income arising on the net investment, which has already been duly recognized under “Other Income” and offered to tax in the return of income.

6.6 It is therefore evident that the accounting and tax treatment adopted by our client is fully aligned with the principle of taxing real income. While the finance income component has already been subjected to tax, the principal recovery does not fall within the ambit of taxable income under the Ordinance. Accordingly, there is no element of income which has either been understated or escaped taxation.

6.7 The approach adopted in the notice, whereby the entire amount has been viewed as a reduction from revenue and proposed to be added back in isolation, disregards the underlying bifurcation and corresponding recognition of income. Such an approach leads to a distorted computation of taxable income, as it effectively seeks to tax a capital recovery while ignoring the fact that the revenue component has already been brought to tax.

6.8 It is further submitted that the presentation in the financial statements, whereby gross billing is adjusted to exclude capital recovery, is merely a matter of appropriate disclosure to reflect true operational revenue. This presentation does not, in any manner, result in suppression or understatement of income, as the net impact on the profit and loss account—comprising finance income and amortization—has already been duly accounted for.

6.9 In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the amount in question represents recovery under a lease-type arrangement with proper bifurcation between capital and revenue components in accordance with internationally accepted accounting principles. The finance income has already been offered to tax, while the principal component represents capital recovery and is not taxable. The proposed addition of Rs. 215,637,000, being based on an incorrect appreciation of facts and law, is therefore unsustainable and liable to be dropped in entirety.

This notice has been issued in response to our earlier submission vide letter No. DT 3987 dated April 15, 2026. Through the said clarification notice, your good office has required our client to furnish explanation and supporting documentation with respect to the details earlier provided in response to the information sought under Rule 44(4) of the Income Tax Rules, 2002.

Below is a refined and comprehensive response, aligned with the notice and supported by the Supreme Court judgment you shared:

---

**Subject: Response to Notice under Section 161(1A) – Clarification on Limitation and Alleged Pending Proceedings**

Dear Sir,

We refer to the subject notice issued under section 161(1A) read with sections 182 and 205 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, wherein it has been observed that the limitation prescribed under section 174(3) is not applicable on the premise that proceedings under Rule 44(4) read with section 161 were pending.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the above understanding is based on an incorrect appreciation of both the factual and legal position. The analogy drawn in the notice, linking Rule 44(4) with section 161 so as to suggest the existence of “pending proceedings”, is misconceived and not supported by the scheme of the law.

In this regard, it is important to clarify that Rule 44(4) of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 does not, in itself, constitute an independent or substantive proceeding. It is merely an enabling provision for seeking reconciliation statements or information, typically invoked in conjunction with section 176 of the Ordinance. Such a notice is purely informational in nature and cannot be equated with adjudicatory proceedings. Therefore, any suggestion that a Rule 44(4) notice—by itself—creates or sustains “pending proceedings” is legally untenable.

The correct legal position, as consistently recognized, is that a notice under Rule 44(4) read with section 176 is only a preliminary step for gathering information. It is only after the taxpayer furnishes the requisite details that the Department may, if considered necessary, initiate formal proceedings under section 161. Consequently, Rule 44 proceedings cannot be read with section 161, nor can they be treated as proceedings pending under section 161.

In the present case, no proceedings under section 161 were initiated within the statutory time frame. In fact, the very first notice under section 161 was issued on 15 April 2026 fileciteturn0file0, which is clearly beyond the limitation period envisaged under section 174(3) of the Ordinance. As such, there were no “pending proceedings” in existence prior to the expiry of the six-year limitation period that could trigger the exception provided in the proviso to section 174(3).

The reliance placed in the notice on the judgment of the Honourable Supreme Court in the case of *CIR Zone-IV Lahore vs Panther Sports & Rubber Industries (Pvt.) Ltd.* is also misplaced. A plain reading of the said judgment shows that the principle laid down therein actually supports the taxpayer’s position. The Honourable Court has categorically held that a taxpayer is only required to maintain records for six years and cannot be compelled to produce records beyond this statutory period. It has further been clarified that although notices under sections 161, 165 or Rule 44(4) may not carry an express limitation, they cannot be given effect to once the period under section 174(3) has lapsed, as the taxpayer is no longer under any legal obligation to maintain such records fileciteturn0file1.

More importantly, the Honourable Supreme Court also clarified that the exception relating to “pending proceedings” applies only where valid proceedings are already in existence within the limitation period. In the absence of such proceedings, the protection under section 174(3) remains fully available to the taxpayer. In the instant case, since no proceedings under section 161 were initiated within the prescribed timeframe, the said exception is not attracted.

It is further pertinent to note that the departmental appeal in the aforesaid case was dismissed by the Honourable Supreme Court, thereby affirming the principle that notices seeking compliance beyond the statutory record retention period are ineffective and unenforceable. Therefore, reliance on this judgment to justify continuation of time-barred proceedings is contrary to the very ratio decidendi of the case.

In view of the above, it is respectfully submitted that:

- There were no proceedings pending within the meaning of section 174(3) prior to the expiry of limitation;
- Rule 44(4) proceedings are merely informational and cannot be equated with or read alongside section 161 proceedings;
- The first valid notice under section 161 having been issued after the expiry of the statutory period is clearly time-barred; and
- The reliance placed on the Supreme Court judgment is misconceived, as the same, in fact, supports the taxpayer’s position.

Accordingly, the proceedings initiated under section 161(1A) are without lawful authority and liable to be dropped.

We trust the above clarifies the legal and factual position. However, should any further clarification be required, we shall be pleased to assist.

Yours faithfully,  
[Name]

Here is a more detailed and fully developed response, with a stronger legal narrative and reproduction of the operative portion of the Supreme Court judgment, all kept in refined paragraph form:

---

**Subject: Detailed Response to Notice under Section 161(1A) – Limitation and Misplaced Reliance on “Pending Proceedings”**

Dear Sir,

We refer to the subject notice issued under section 161(1A) read with sections 182 and 205 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, wherein it has been contended that the limitation prescribed under section 174(3) is inapplicable on the premise that proceedings under Rule 44(4) read with section 161 were pending. We further note that reliance has been placed on the judgment of the Honourable Supreme Court in the case of *CIR Zone-IV Lahore vs Panther Sports & Rubber Industries (Pvt.) Ltd.* to support this position.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the above conclusion is based on a fundamental misapprehension of both facts and law. The entire premise of the notice hinges on the assumption that proceedings under Rule 44(4) can be read with section 161 and, on that basis, treated as “pending proceedings” so as to invoke the exception to section 174(3). This assumption is legally unsustainable.

Rule 44(4) of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 is not an independent charging or adjudicatory provision. It is merely an enabling mechanism through which reconciliation or statements may be called for, generally read in conjunction with section 176 of the Ordinance. Such notices are purely informational in character and are issued for the purpose of verification or reconciliation of data. They do not, by themselves, initiate any proceedings determining liability, nor do they carry any adjudicatory consequence. It is a well-settled proposition, including as recognized in various judicial precedents of the superior courts, that such informational notices cannot be equated with “proceedings” for the purposes of invoking statutory exceptions relating to limitation.

In fact, the statutory scheme clearly demonstrates a sequential process: first, information may be called through Rule 44 read with section 176; thereafter, upon examination of such information, if any default is identified, only then can proceedings under section 161 be validly initiated. Therefore, Rule 44(4) cannot be read “with” section 161 in the manner suggested in the notice. The two operate at distinct stages, and conflating them to artificially create the existence of “pending proceedings” is contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance.

In the present case, no proceedings under section 161 were initiated within the limitation period prescribed under section 174(3). The record clearly shows that the first notice under section 161 was issued on 15 April 2026 fileciteturn0file0, which is admittedly beyond the six-year statutory period. Therefore, as on the date of expiry of limitation, there were no valid or subsisting proceedings pending against the taxpayer. Consequently, the exception contained in the proviso to section 174(3) is not attracted in the instant case.

The reliance placed on the judgment of the Honourable Supreme Court in *Panther Sports* is, with utmost respect, misplaced. A plain reading of the judgment shows that it does not support the Department’s position; rather, it unequivocally reinforces the taxpayer’s case. The Honourable Supreme Court, while dismissing the Department’s petition, has laid down the following operative principle:

> “We hold that a taxpayer is obliged to maintain the record under section 174(3) of the Ordinance for a period of six years and the taxpayer cannot be compelled to produce the record for a tax year beyond the period of six years as stipulated in section 174(3) of the Ordinance. Hence notices issued under section 165(2B) or 161(1A) of the Ordinance being ineffective and unenforceable are set aside.” fileciteturn0file1  

Further, the Honourable Court elaborated the statutory scheme in clear terms and held that although certain provisions may not prescribe a specific limitation period, they cannot be given effect once the statutory timeframe under section 174(3) has expired, as the taxpayer is no longer under any legal obligation to maintain or produce records beyond such period. fileciteturn0file1

Importantly, the exception relating to “pending proceedings” was also addressed in the judgment, wherein it was clarified that such exception applies only where valid proceedings are already in existence within the limitation period. The said exception cannot be invoked retrospectively or artificially created by linking informational notices with adjudicatory provisions. In the absence of legally cognizable proceedings prior to the expiry of limitation, the protection available to the taxpayer under section 174(3) remains intact.

It is also relevant to highlight that the Department’s petition in the aforesaid case was dismissed, thereby affirming the view of the Honourable High Court that notices seeking compliance beyond the statutory period are unlawful and unenforceable. Therefore, it is inconceivable how a judgment that has culminated in dismissal of the Department’s position can now be relied upon to support an interpretation that effectively negates the statutory protection granted to taxpayers.

Without prejudice, it is further submitted that even from a practical standpoint, treating Rule 44(4) notices as “pending proceedings” would defeat the very purpose of section 174(3). The law consciously balances the rights of the taxpayer and the powers of the Department by imposing a six-year record retention obligation. Allowing informational queries to indefinitely extend this period would render the statutory protection meaningless, which is precisely what the Honourable Supreme Court has cautioned against.

In light of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that there were no proceedings pending within the meaning of section 174(3) at the relevant time; that Rule 44(4) notices are purely informational and cannot be equated with proceedings under section 161; and that the initiation of proceedings under section 161 after expiry of the statutory period is clearly time-barred and without lawful authority.

Accordingly, the instant proceedings are liable to be dropped in limine.

We trust the above sufficiently clarifies the position. However, should your good office require any further clarification, we shall be pleased to provide the same.

Yours faithfully,  
[Name]

---

**Subject:** Clarification on Inconsistency Point & Request for Records

Dear Ikra,

I hope you are doing well. Thank you for your email.

I would like to clarify a point from my earlier correspondence regarding the inconsistency highlighted. The reference to inconsistency was intended in the context of the tax department’s approach and not at the level of the Commissioner (Appeals). The concern essentially relates to the differing treatment adopted by the department across tax years 2015 and 2016 on the same underlying subject matter. In one instance, particularly in the audit proceedings involving a broader scope, the department has taken a position to capitalize the amount, whereas in proceedings under section 122(5A) read with section 108, a disallowance has been proposed. This clearly reflects an inconsistent departmental stance, which ideally should be brought on record before the Tribunal as part of our arguments to demonstrate lack of uniformity in treatment.

Ideally, this ground should have been specifically raised at the Commissioner (Appeals) stage; however, from a review of the appellate order, it does not appear that the matter has been captured either in the grounds of appeal or explicitly addressed in the order. That said, it is quite possible that the contention may have been discussed during the course of proceedings, even if not formally documented.

Now that additional grounds have been filed, we would request you to kindly share the acknowledged copy for our record. Furthermore, if there is any information or documentation required from our end in relation to tax years 2015 and 2016, please let us know. It would also be helpful if you could share the complete set of details for both years from scratch, so that we may independently review the position and provide any further input or assistance, if required, in a timely manner.

Please feel free to reach out in case of any clarification.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

**Subject:** Clarification Required – Non-Submission of Reconciliation and Way Forward  

Dear Najam,  

Thank you for your email. I would like to refer back to our earlier meeting held at A.F. Ferguson, where the matter was discussed in detail with your seniors and our entire team. While I am not certain whether you were present in that meeting, the clear conclusion reached at that time was that the reconciliation—once prepared and shared—would be duly submitted before the Commissioner (Appeals), irrespective of the hearing status. This approach was agreed considering the sensitive nature of the case, particularly in the context of PICT, and the need to strengthen our position on factual grounds. It was also mutually acknowledged that even though the case remains strong on merits, it was important to place detailed reconciliations and supporting invoices on record to counter any perception that no substantive documentation had been provided by the taxpayer.  

In this background, it is quite concerning that despite the reconciliation and sample invoices being shared with you on a timely basis, the same were not formally submitted through a written filing before the Commissioner (Appeals). As you are aware, the order appears to have been passed on a backdated basis around 23 March 2026, and timely submission of these documents could have materially supported our case at higher appellate forums by demonstrating that relevant evidence was available but not considered. I would therefore appreciate a clear explanation as to why these submissions were not made, particularly when the understanding was that hearings and submissions were to be treated as separate matters, and filings were to be ensured regardless of hearing scheduling.  

Further, with respect to your comments on the reconciliation, I must highlight that the position taken appears to be based on an incomplete appreciation of the workings shared. The FTS component, in particular, has not been fully analyzed. As reflected in the reconciliation shared yesterday, certain portions of the liability have been discharged as a withholding agent—especially in the earlier quarters—whereas the officer has proceeded primarily on Annex-C figures. This has resulted in excessive adjustments, as the officer has reduced amounts already discharged under a different mechanism. Therefore, the issue is not of timing difference but rather of incorrect reconciliation methodology applied at the assessment stage. I would strongly suggest that this be re-evaluated internally with your seniors, as the reconciliation clearly addresses these aspects.  

It is also pertinent to note that two key actions appear to have been missed at our end: firstly, the formal submission of reconciliation and supporting documents before the Commissioner (Appeals), and secondly, the filing of revised grounds based on a proper appreciation of the reconciliation. Both these aspects are critical from a litigation strategy perspective, particularly when the matter proceeds to the Tribunal.  

Given the importance of the matter, I would suggest that we arrange a call at the earliest to discuss these issues in detail, align on the correct factual position, and determine the appropriate course of action going forward. Please let me know your availability so that we can schedule this discussion promptly.  

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

Engagement Objective: To conduct a comprehensive review of the Profit and Loss account for the partnership from its inception through July 2025, ensuring the accuracy, completeness, and fair presentation of financial performance.
Detailed Scope of Work
Revenue and Procurement Cycle Evaluation

Financial Statement Classification Analysis
Analyze the classification of income and expenditure items to ensure compliance with relevant accounting frameworks and to confirm that all items are mapped to the correct ledger accounts.
Substantive Testing of Expenses
Using a risk-based materiality threshold, perform detailed verification of underlying documentation (invoices, receipts, and contracts) for significant expense categories to validate the authenticity and business purpose of each transaction.
Cost Apportionment and Allocation Review
Critically assess the methodologies used for apportioning joint or indirect costs. This ensures that the basis of apportionment is consistent, reasonable, and reflective of the actual resource consumption within the textile operations.
Completeness and Cut-off Procedures
Execute targeted audit procedures to identify potential unrecorded sales, purchases, or accrued expenses. This includes testing "cut-off" points to ensure transactions are recorded in the correct accounting period.
External Circularization and Supplier Verification
Perform external balance confirmations for major suppliers to reconcile internal records with third-party data.
Payment and Disbursement Validation
Review the payment cycle to verify that disbursements made to suppliers are properly authorized, accurately recorded, and supported by valid evidence of delivery/service.

Dear [Client Name],  

Thank you for your time during the discussion.

As understood, entity["company","Oxford SMC","Pakistan entity"] has an arrangement with entity["organization","University of Oxford","UK"] under which a brand fee is charged by the UK entity to the SMC. Commercially, it has been agreed that while withholding income tax may be deducted from the invoice value and the net amount remitted, the corresponding Sindh Sales Tax (SST) liability—arising due to the non-resident status of the service provider—is to be borne by the SMC itself and not adjusted against the payable amount to the UK entity.

Your primary query relates to whether the SST paid under the reverse charge mechanism constitutes an admissible expense for income tax purposes. In this regard, it is important to consider that the tax has been discharged at the full rate under the reverse charge mechanism prescribed under the entity["law","Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011","SSTSA"]. However, as highlighted during the discussion, the prescribed procedural framework—such as proper registration, declaration, and alignment with the input/output tax adjustment mechanism—has not been fully followed. Consequently, the corresponding input tax has neither been claimed nor is it currently available for adjustment.

From an income tax perspective under the entity["law","Income Tax Ordinance, 2001","Pakistan"], the allowability of such expense depends on its nature and whether it is wholly and exclusively incurred for business purposes. While SST typically forms part of cost where it is irrecoverable, a distinction arises in cases where the tax is paid at full rate and a statutory mechanism exists for its adjustment or refund. In such situations, the tax authorities may take a position that the amount does not represent a final cost but rather a recoverable input tax, and therefore should not be allowed as a deductible expense.

In your specific case, since the SST has been discharged at the full rate under reverse charge, there is a reasonable likelihood that the department may challenge its admissibility as an expense. The contention could be that the amount ought to have been either adjusted against output tax (subject to proper compliance with procedural requirements) or claimed through the refund mechanism, instead of being treated as a direct charge to the profit and loss account.

Accordingly, while a position may be taken that the tax represents a cost due to its practical non-recoverability in the current circumstances, the exposure remains that the same could be disallowed during assessment proceedings on the grounds discussed above.

We would recommend evaluating the possibility of regularizing the SST position going forward—particularly in terms of compliance with the prescribed reverse charge procedures—to mitigate this risk.

**Response to Notice – Tax Year 2024**

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the observation contained in the notice does not refer to any specific provision of the entity["law","Income Tax Ordinance, 2001","Pakistan tax law"] under which the proposed addition of Rs. 64,168,000 is sought to be made. The proposed adjustment appears to be based on a mechanical comparison between figures disclosed in different notes to the financial statements, without appreciating the nature and tax treatment of the underlying transaction. In absence of a charging or disallowance provision, the proposed addition lacks legal basis and is therefore not sustainable.

Without prejudice to the above, it is submitted that the amount of Rs. 215,637,000 does not represent revenue or income of the Company. The same relates to recovery of construction cost of the SSGC branch pipeline along with an embedded financing component, arising under the LNG Services Agreement executed with SSGC. Under this arrangement, the Company constructed the pipeline and subsequently transferred the same to SSGC, with recovery structured through periodic billing. Accordingly, the transaction is not in the nature of sale or service revenue but represents a structured recovery of investment along with finance income.

In line with applicable accounting principles, the arrangement has been treated akin to a financing/lease arrangement, whereby the total recovery comprises two distinct components: (i) principal recovery (capital component), and (ii) finance/interest income. For the year under consideration, the finance income component amounting to Rs. 151,469,000 has already been recognized under “other income” and duly offered to tax. The balance amount of Rs. 64,168,000 represents recovery of principal, which is purely capital in nature and does not fall within the ambit of taxable income.

The observation in the notice that the difference should be added back effectively proceeds on the assumption that the entire amount deducted from gross revenue must reconcile with taxable income. This approach is fundamentally flawed, as it disregards the settled principle that only real income, and not capital recovery, is subject to tax. The principal component cannot be taxed merely because it is presented as a reduction from gross billing for disclosure purposes.

With respect to the reference made to depreciation on the pipeline, it is respectfully clarified that the accounting and tax treatment of depreciation is independent of the recovery mechanism. The claim of tax depreciation, if any, is governed by specific provisions of the Ordinance relating to ownership, use, and classification of assets. The recovery of capital through billing does not convert such recovery into income, nor does it trigger any automatic disallowance or addition. There is no provision in law which mandates that principal recovery must be offered to tax merely because depreciation has been claimed.

Furthermore, the linkage drawn by your good office between the deduction from revenue and the “other income” figure reflects an incomplete appreciation of the accounting treatment. The finance income component has already been recognized and taxed separately, whereas the principal recovery has been excluded from revenue to avoid overstatement of operational income. Any attempt to recompute income by aggregating these figures would result in double counting of the same stream and distortion of taxable income.

It is also respectfully submitted that such an approach is inconsistent with the principle of taxing net real income and would effectively lead to taxation of capital receipts, which is neither contemplated nor permitted under the law. The treatment adopted by the Company ensures that only the financing element is subjected to tax, which is fully in line with established tax principles and accounting standards.

In view of the above, it is submitted that the proposed addition of Rs. 64,168,000 is based on a misinterpretation of facts and law, and therefore, the same may kindly be dropped.

The finance income component amounting to Rs. 151,469,000 has been duly recognized under “other income” and offered to tax. The remaining amount of Rs. 64,168,000 represents recovery of principal, which is capital in nature and does not constitute income chargeable to tax.

The inference drawn in the notice, whereby the difference between the total recovery and the finance income has been proposed for addition, is based on an incorrect premise that the entire deduction from revenue must reconcile with taxable income. **Response to Notice – Tax Year 2024**

We refer to the subject notice wherein your good office has observed that an amount of Rs. 215,637,000 deducted from gross revenue on account of recovery of construction cost of SSGC branch pipeline, along with related interest, has not been fully offered to tax. On the basis of a comparison with the interest income of Rs. 151,469,000 disclosed under “other income”, it has been inferred that the differential amount of Rs. 64,168,000 is liable to be added back to total income, particularly in view of the claim of tax depreciation on the said pipeline.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the observation contained in the notice does not identify any specific charging or disallowance provision of the entity["law","Income Tax Ordinance, 2001","Pakistan tax law"] under which the proposed addition is sought to be made. The proposed adjustment appears to be based on a perceived mismatch between figures disclosed in different notes to the financial statements, without undertaking any examination of the nature, substance, and tax characterization of the underlying transaction. It is a settled position of law that income can only be brought to tax under an express charging provision, and in absence thereof, no addition can be sustained merely on the basis of accounting presentation or perceived inconsistencies. On this ground alone, the proposed addition is not legally tenable.

Without prejudice to the above, it is submitted that the amount of Rs. 215,637,000 does not represent revenue or business income of the Company. The same pertains to recovery associated with the SSGC branch pipeline constructed pursuant to the LNG Services Agreement with SSGC. Under this arrangement, the Company was contractually obligated to construct a dedicated pipeline infrastructure, which upon commissioning was effectively transferred for operational use, with the recovery of cost structured through periodic billing over the tenure of the arrangement.

The substance of the arrangement is that of a financing structure rather than a revenue-generating activity. In economic terms, the Company has made an upfront investment in the construction of the pipeline, and the subsequent recoveries represent a combination of return of that investment (principal) and a financing return (interest). This treatment is consistent with applicable accounting principles, under which such arrangements are treated akin to a net investment in a lease or financing arrangement, rather than outright revenue.

In line with the above, the total recovery of Rs. 215,637,000 has been appropriately bifurcated based on its underlying economic substance. The finance/interest component amounting to Rs. 151,469,000 has been duly recognized under “other income” and offered to tax in the return of income. The balance amount of Rs. 64,168,000 represents recovery of principal, which is purely capital in nature and does not constitute income chargeable to tax under the Ordinance. It is respectfully emphasized that recovery of capital does not give rise to taxable income, as it merely represents recoupment of an investment already made.

The approach adopted in the notice, whereby the differential amount has been proposed to be added back, effectively proceeds on the assumption that the entire deduction from gross revenue must reconcile with taxable income. This assumption is fundamentally flawed, as it disregards the settled principle of taxation of real income. The accounting presentation, whereby gross billing is reduced to exclude the capital recovery component, is intended solely to reflect the true operational revenue and avoid overstatement. Such presentation cannot be interpreted to mean that the excluded amount represents taxable income.

Further, the linkage drawn with the claim of tax depreciation on the pipeline is misplaced and legally unsustainable. The allowability of depreciation is governed by specific provisions of the Ordinance relating to ownership, use, and classification of depreciable assets. The treatment of depreciation operates independently of the recovery mechanism adopted for the underlying asset. There is no provision in the Ordinance which requires that principal recovery be treated as income merely because depreciation has been claimed on the asset. Any such inference would amount to introducing a condition not contemplated under the law.

Moreover, the approach adopted in the notice results in an inherent distortion of taxable income. While the finance income component has already been duly subjected to tax, the proposed addition seeks to bring to tax the principal recovery as well, thereby effectively taxing both the return on investment and the return of investment. This leads to double counting of the same economic stream, which is contrary to fundamental tax principles and well-established jurisprudence.

It is also respectfully submitted that the figures disclosed in the financial statements have been presented in accordance with applicable accounting standards, and the bifurcation between finance income and principal recovery has been transparently disclosed. The tax treatment adopted by the Company is fully aligned with such disclosure and ensures that only the income component is subjected to tax. There is, therefore, no suppression, understatement, or mischaracterization of income.

In view of the foregoing, it is evident that the proposed addition of Rs. 64,168,000 is based on an incomplete appreciation of the facts and an incorrect application of tax principles. The amount represents capital recovery, which falls outside the ambit of taxable income, and the corresponding finance income has already been duly offered to tax. Accordingly, no part of the said amount is liable to be added back to total income.

**In light of the above, it is respectfully requested that the proposed addition may kindly be dropped in full, as the treatment adopted by the Company is both legally sustainable and consistent with the principle of taxing only real income.**

**Subject: Post-Merger Tax Compliance Roadmap – ICL (Non-Surviving) & SGL (Surviving Entity)**  

Dear [Client Name],  

I hope you are doing well.  

We refer to the merger of Industrial Clothing Limited (ICL) into Shahbaz Garments Limited (SGL), duly approved by the Court, with an effective date of January 1, 2025. We understand that ICL is the non-surviving entity, while SGL is the surviving entity, and that ICL’s return for Tax Year 2025 (covering the period January to December 2024) has already been filed. In light of these facts, the post-merger compliance requirements need to be carefully aligned with the legal and procedural framework rather than following a generic discontinuance approach.  

From an income tax standpoint, since the merger has taken effect from January 1, 2025, and the last return of ICL has already been filed up to December 31, 2024, technically no further return is required to be filed for ICL under section 114 read with section 117 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. However, it remains important to formally document the cessation of ICL’s independent tax status and ensure that the merger is appropriately reflected in the tax records. In practice, this involves updating the profile on IRIS, ensuring that no further compliance obligations (including withholding statements under section 165 or advance tax under section 147) remain linked to ICL post-merger, and aligning all historical tax credits, refunds, and proceedings with the successor entity, i.e., SGL.  

The merger itself should be evaluated under section 97A of the Ordinance to ensure that the tax neutrality conditions are fully satisfied, particularly with respect to transfer of assets and liabilities at tax written down values, continuity of ownership, and absence of immediate tax implications. The accounting treatment adopted by SGL must also be consistent with this position, as any deviation (for example, revaluation or recognition of gains) could trigger tax exposure. Further, any brought forward business losses or unabsorbed depreciation of ICL may only be available to SGL subject to the conditions prescribed under section 57A, including continuity of business and shareholding thresholds, which should be assessed in detail before any such claim is incorporated in SGL’s future returns.  

From a withholding tax perspective, a complete transition needs to be ensured whereby all withholding obligations post January 1, 2025 are discharged solely under SGL’s NTN. This includes vendor payments under section 153, salary withholding under section 149, rent under section 155, and other applicable provisions such as sections 231A, 231B, 236G and 236H. Any contracts, vendor master data, payroll systems, and banking arrangements still reflecting ICL’s NTN should be immediately updated to avoid mismatches in IRIS and exposure during withholding tax audits.  

On the sales tax side, the position requires careful handling under section 21 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 11 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006. Since ICL has ceased to exist as a taxable person post-merger, a formal de-registration process should be initiated. Prior to filing the de-registration application (STR-3), it is critical to ensure that all sales tax returns up to December 2024 have been filed, and that output tax, input tax, carried forward balances, and any outstanding liabilities are fully reconciled. The law empowers the Commissioner to conduct an audit or seek further clarification before approving de-registration, and no input tax adjustment or refund can be claimed once the de-registration process is initiated, which makes timing and reconciliation particularly important.  

Simultaneously, SGL’s sales tax registration profile must be updated to reflect the merged operations. This includes amendment of business particulars, addition of business premises (if ICL’s locations are being retained), and alignment of all invoicing, contracts, and supply chains under SGL’s STRN from January 1, 2025 onward. Any invoices issued under ICL’s registration after the effective date may create complications both for SGL and its customers, particularly in terms of input tax admissibility and audit exposure.  

In addition to the above, it is essential to review all ongoing proceedings, audits, or litigation relating to ICL. As a matter of law and practice, SGL, being the successor entity, may be required to assume responsibility for such matters. Accordingly, appropriate intimations should be made to the relevant tax authorities wherever proceedings are pending, enclosing the Court order approving the merger and clarifying the successor status of SGL.  

From a practical standpoint, we recommend that a consolidated post-merger compliance file be maintained, including the Court order, merger scheme, asset and liability transfer schedules, tax depreciation records, sales tax reconciliations, withholding tax records, and correspondence with authorities. This will be critical in defending the position during any future audit or assessment proceedings.  

In light of the above, we request you to share the Court order and any supporting merger documentation so that we may perform a detailed technical review and advise on any further refinements required in the compliance approach. Based on this, we will also prepare a step-wise implementation plan to ensure that all regulatory requirements are fully met and aligned with the law.  

Please feel free to reach out in case you would like us to walk you through the above in detail.  

Best regards,

Non-compliance may expose the return to being treated as invalid or incomplete, which should be strictly avoided.
