The merger does not constitute discontinuance under section 117 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, as the business has not ceased but has been transferred to SGL. Since ICL’s return up to December 31, 2024 has already been filed, there is no requirement to file any additional or final return.  

All post-merger financial and tax results from January 1, 2025 onwards will be reported in SGL’s return for Tax Year 2026. Accordingly, there is no separate income tax return filing requirement arising due to the merger itself.

**Subject: Post-Merger Tax Compliance Roadmap – ICL Industrial Grouping Merger into XDL Limited**

Dear [Client Name],

I hope you are doing well.

We understand that the merger of ICL Industrial Grouping into XDL Limited has become effective from January 1, 2025. In view of the said merger, we consider it important to undertake a detailed post-merger tax compliance review so that all consequential actions under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, Income Tax Rules, 2002, Sales Tax Act, 1990 and Sales Tax Rules, 2006 are identified, documented and implemented in a timely manner.

From an income tax perspective, the merger needs to be examined under the provisions dealing with tax-neutral restructuring, particularly section 97A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, which provides non-recognition treatment for disposal of assets under a scheme of arrangement and reconstruction, subject to prescribed conditions, including approval of the scheme by the High Court, SECP or other relevant authority, as applicable. Accordingly, we would need to review the approved merger scheme, effective date, vesting order, transfer of assets and liabilities, accounting entries, tax written down values, stock values, intangibles, and any consideration or share issuance arising from the merger.

Further, if the merging entity has any assessed business losses or unabsorbed depreciation, the position would need to be evaluated under section 57A of the Ordinance. The said provision allows set-off of business loss consequent to amalgamation, subject to conditions, including continuity of business for the prescribed period. Therefore, a separate schedule of brought-forward losses, unabsorbed depreciation, minimum tax, advance tax, tax credits, and any pending refunds should be prepared for determining what can validly be carried forward or claimed by XDL Limited after the merger.

Since the business of ICL Industrial Grouping has discontinued due to merger, a notice of discontinuance should also be considered under section 117 of the Ordinance. The law requires intimation to the Commissioner within fifteen days of discontinuance, and the Commissioner may require filing of a return for the period commencing from the first day of the tax year up to the date of discontinuance. Accordingly, a final / short-period income tax return for the merging entity may need to be prepared up to December 31, 2024, while XDL Limited should incorporate the post-merger results from January 1, 2025 onward in its own tax records and annual return.

In addition, the return filing position under sections 114, 118 and 120 of the Ordinance should be mapped carefully. This would include preparation of separate tax computations for the pre-merger period, reconciliation of accounting profit with taxable income, treatment of assets transferred at tax written down value, continuity of depreciation under sections 22, 23 and 24, treatment of stock-in-trade under section 35, and reconciliation of any withholding taxes deducted or collected in the name of the merging entity before the effective date.

The withholding tax profile also needs to be reviewed in detail. This includes all obligations under sections 149, 153, 155, 156, 231A, 231B, 236G, 236H and other applicable withholding provisions, depending on the nature of transactions. Any tax deducted before the effective date should remain properly reconciled with the NTN of the merging entity, whereas post-merger deductions and payments should be made under XDL Limited’s NTN. All contracts, vendor master data, customer records, payroll records, banks, utility accounts and tax deduction certificates should be updated to avoid mismatch in IRIS.

From a sales tax perspective, the position should be reviewed under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 and Sales Tax Rules, 2006. Since the merging entity ceases to carry on business independently, sales tax de-registration or cancellation of registration should be considered under section 21 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 11 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006. As per the current procedure, the application for de-registration is required to be filed online through the computerized system in Form STR-3. The Commissioner may examine the record, conduct inquiry or audit, require discharge of outstanding liabilities, and direct filing of a final return under section 28 before completion of de-registration.

Before applying for sales tax de-registration, all monthly sales tax returns up to the effective date should be filed under section 26 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The output tax, input tax, debit / credit notes, withholding sales tax, stock position, fixed assets, open advances, unadjusted input tax, and carried-forward balances should be reconciled. Particular care is required because Rule 11 restricts input tax adjustment or refund during the currency of de-registration, and invoices issued after the online de-registration application may create issues for both the merging entity and its customers.

In case any sales tax registration, business activity, branch, manufacturing unit, or principal activity is required to be continued under XDL Limited, the particulars of XDL Limited should be amended on IRIS / FBR systems. This includes change in business description, addition of business premises, addition or deletion of bank accounts, principal activity codes, authorized representatives, and branch / unit details. If there are multiple registrations or overlapping registrations, Rule 10 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 regarding cancellation of multiple registrations may also become relevant.

Operationally, the client should also ensure that all post-merger invoices, sales tax invoices, purchase orders, contracts, delivery challans, import documents, utility bills, bank accounts, POS / ERP profiles, and vendor / customer records are issued and maintained in the name and tax registration particulars of XDL Limited from January 1, 2025 onward. Any invoice issued under the old registration after the effective date may create input tax, withholding tax and audit complications.

We would also recommend preparing a complete post-merger tax compliance file, comprising the approved merger scheme, SECP / Court approval, board and shareholder resolutions, effective date confirmation, list of assets and liabilities transferred, tax WDV schedules, stock reconciliation, debtor and creditor schedules, withholding tax challans, sales tax returns, final return working, pending litigation details, refund details, bank account closure / transfer documents, and correspondence with FBR / relevant authorities.

In view of the above, we request you to kindly share the following documents and information so that we may review the position and prepare a detailed step-wise compliance roadmap:

the approved merger scheme and regulatory approval order; effective date confirmation; audited / management accounts up to December 31, 2024; tax depreciation schedules; brought-forward loss and depreciation position; sales tax return copies up to the effective date; details of unadjusted input tax or refunds; list of pending income tax and sales tax proceedings; withholding tax statements filed before and after the merger; details of open contracts, bank accounts, branches, registrations, and any invoices issued after January 1, 2025 under the old registration.

Once the above information is reviewed, we will be able to advise on the exact filings, intimations, applications, reconciliations and correspondence required to regularize the post-merger tax position and avoid future exposure during audit or assessment proceedings.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

Hi Nabiel, we hope you are doing well.

We refer to the merger of Industrial Clothing Limited (ICL) into Shahbaz Garments Limited (SGL), duly sanctioned by the Sindh High Court, with an effective date of January 1, 2025. We understand that ICL is the non-surviving entity, while SGL is the surviving entity. Further, the income tax return of ICL for Tax Year 2025 (covering the financial year ended December 31, 2024) has already been filed; however, the same was submitted without audited financial statements, as the accounts are still under finalization and signing.

At this stage, approximately one month has already elapsed, leaving a limited window of around one month and a few days to regularize this position without requiring approval from the Commissioner. It is therefore critical that the audited accounts are finalized and uploaded within this prescribed timeframe. In case of delay, we may be constrained to either submit the accounts separately or revisit the return position through an appropriate corrective course; however, such alternatives are not ideal and may expose the return to being treated as incomplete. This risk should be avoided through timely compliance.

**INCOME TAX IMPLICATIONS**

**Filing Position and Post-Merger Continuity**

From an income tax perspective, the merger does not constitute a discontinuance of business under section 117 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Rather, it represents a transfer of business under a court-approved scheme, with continuity maintained in the hands of SGL. Since ICL’s return has already been filed up to December 31, 2024, there is no requirement to file any further return on its behalf. All income, assets, and obligations from January 1, 2025 onwards will form part of SGL’s tax profile for Tax Year 2026.

As a matter of good practice, we recommend that an intimation be filed with the concerned Commissioner, enclosing the Court order and clearly documenting that the business of ICL has been merged into SGL. While not mandatory, this helps align the tax department’s records and avoids unnecessary procedural queries in future.

**Withholding Tax Alignment and Credit Transition**

From a withholding tax standpoint, immediate corrective action is required. Due to the timing gap in receipt and implementation of the merger order, it is likely that withholding tax deductions post January 1, 2025 may have continued under ICL’s NTN. All customers and counterparties should be formally notified to deduct withholding tax in the name and NTN of SGL going forward.

Further, withholding tax credits already deposited under ICL’s NTN for the post-merger period will need to be transferred to SGL. This typically involves CPR corrections and coordination with the relevant tax offices. Given that ICL and SGL fall under different jurisdictions, this process will require structured engagement with both Commissioners. Based on experience, early initiation is essential to avoid blockage of credits at the time of assessment.

**Transfer of Tax Profiles, Assets and Contracts**

Pursuant to the merger, all tax profiles, business assets, and contractual positions of ICL should effectively stand transitioned to SGL. This includes factory premises, leases, rental agreements, utilities, and all customer and vendor contracts. Necessary amendments or novation agreements should be executed where required to reflect SGL as the contracting party.

From a tax registration standpoint, all operational activities must now be aligned with SGL’s NTN and STRN. No transactions should be routed through ICL going forward, as it no longer exists as a separate taxable person.

**Payroll and Employee Transition**

All employees previously on ICL’s payroll should be formally transferred to SGL. Payroll processing, salary disbursements, and withholding tax compliance under section 149 must now be carried out under SGL. Any residual payroll activity under ICL should be discontinued to avoid inconsistencies in tax reporting.

**SALES TAX IMPLICATIONS**

**De-Registration Strategy**

While ICL would ordinarily be required to apply for de-registration under section 21 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 11 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, we recommend deferring this step at present. This is due to the practical limitation that input tax balances lying in ICL cannot be seamlessly transferred to SGL through the existing FBR system. Premature de-registration may therefore result in permanent loss of such input tax.

**Input Tax Management and Invoicing Transition**

A structured approach is required to manage the input tax position of ICL. This may involve obtaining credit notes from suppliers, wherever permissible, and re-routing transactions through SGL. Simultaneously, all sales tax invoicing must now be undertaken under SGL. No further output tax should be generated under ICL, and incoming input tax should be carefully controlled to avoid accumulation.

We would request you to share the ageing of input tax balances so that an appropriate recovery or adjustment strategy can be developed.

**Transfer of Business Assets – Sales Tax Treatment**

In respect of assets lying in ICL’s books, their transfer to SGL under the merger requires careful handling from a sales tax perspective. Under section 49 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (read with relevant rules and established principles), transfer of a business as a going concern pursuant to a court-approved scheme does not attract sales tax, provided that the entire business undertaking is transferred and continuity is maintained.

Accordingly, the transfer of assets from ICL to SGL may be structured as a transfer of business as a going concern, which would not require charging of output tax. However, appropriate documentation must be maintained, including the merger scheme, court order, and internal transfer records, to substantiate this position in case of any audit or proceedings.

**Other Operational and Compliance Considerations**

It is critical that, with immediate effect, all invoicing, payments, banking transactions, and commercial activities are routed exclusively through SGL. Vendors must be instructed to issue invoices in the name of SGL, and all outstanding receivables and payables of ICL should be settled through SGL to ensure consistency with the legal position.

Additionally, any regulatory registrations, licenses, or approvals held in the name of ICL should be reviewed and updated or transferred to SGL wherever required to ensure uninterrupted business operations.

**CONCLUSION**

In summary, while the merger is legally effective from January 1, 2025, the primary focus now is to align all tax, operational, and compliance aspects with this position. Immediate attention is required in areas such as finalization of audited accounts, withholding tax alignment, transition of contracts and payroll, and proper handling of sales tax matters, particularly input tax and asset transfer.

We would be pleased to assist you in implementing the above steps and coordinating with the relevant tax authorities to ensure a smooth and compliant transition.

Best regards,

We understand that ICL is the non-surviving entity, while SGL is the surviving entity, and that ICL’s return for tax year 2025 (covering the period January to December 2024) has already been filed. Nevertheless, the same was submitted without the audited financial statements, as the accounts are currently under finalization and signing process.

It is therefore critical that the audited accounts are finalized and uploaded within this timeline. INCOME TAX IMPLICATION

Filing of Final Return:

Moving to the post-merger position, we understand that pursuant to the Court-approved scheme, ICL stands merged into Shahbaz Garments Limited (SGL) with effect from January 1, 2025. From a legal standpoint, this does not constitute a “discontinuance of business” under section 117 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001; rather, it is a case of business transfer under a merger, where the business continues in the hands of the surviving entity. Furthermore, since the return of ICL has already been filed up to December 31, 2024, there is no residual period for which any additional or final return is required to be filed. The next tax cycle (tax year 2026) will entirely fall within SGL, and all financial and tax positions from January 1, 2025 onwards will form part of SGL’s return to be filed in the normal course.

That said, as a matter of prudence and documentation, we recommend that an intimation letter be submitted to the concerned Commissioner, enclosing the Court order and formally placing on record that the business of ICL has not been discontinued but has been transferred to SGL under an approved merger scheme. This step, while not strictly mandated, helps in aligning departmental records and mitigating any future procedural complications.

Withholding of Income Tax Implication:

From a withholding tax perspective, immediate corrective action is required. Given that the merger order has been received with some delay, it is likely that withholding tax deductions for the period from January 1, 2025 onwards (and possibly continuing even now) are still being made under ICL’s NTN. This position needs to be rectified on priority. All customers, and counterparties must be formally instructed that any future withholding tax deductions, including against any outstanding receivables of ICL, should be made in the name and NTN of SGL.

Further, all withholding tax credits already deposited under ICL’s NTN (for the post-merger period) will need to be transitioned to SGL in order to ensure their admissibility. Practically, this involves correction of CPRs, which is a time-consuming and documentation-intensive process, particularly where multiple transactions are involved. An added complexity in your case is that ICL and SGL fall under different tax office jurisdictions. Accordingly, we will need to engage with both concerned Commissioners to determine the most efficient mechanism, whether corrections are to be processed through ICL’s jurisdiction or coordinated with SGL’s jurisdiction, to transfer these credits. Given our past experience, this process requires careful handling and early initiation to avoid blockage of tax credits in future assessments.

Other Income Tax Implications

Operationally, it is essential that with immediate effect, all invoicing, payments, contracts, and financial transactions are routed exclusively through SGL. Any outstanding liabilities of ICL should also be settled through SGL to ensure consistency with the legal position that ICL no longer exists as a separate entity. Similarly, all vendors must be instructed to issue invoices in the name of SGL only.

From a payroll and HR perspective, all employees previously on ICL’s payroll should be formally transitioned to SGL. This includes issuance of internal communication or transfer letters, alignment of payroll records, and ensuring that all salary payments, benefits, and withholding tax compliances under section 149 are processed under SGL going forward. There should be no residual payroll activity under ICL, neither on record nor in practice.

SALES TAX IMPLICATION

Sales Tax De-Registration

On the sales tax front, while technically ICL would be required to apply for de-registration under section 21 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 11 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, we would strongly advise against initiating this process immediately. This is primarily due to the carried forward input tax balance lying in ICL, for which there is currently no practical or system-based mechanism available on IRIS to transfer such balances to the surviving entity post-merger. As you are aware, even in similar cases, the matter has required intervention from High Court levels, including directions to the Chairman FBR, and remains operationally challenging.

Carryforward of Input Tax and Invoicing

Accordingly, our recommendation is to first manage and reduce the input tax exposure at ICL’s level. This may involve, where feasible, obtaining credit notes from suppliers (within the permissible time limits) and re-routing such transactions through SGL. Simultaneously, all current and future sales tax invoicing must be carried out under SGL with immediate effect. No further output tax should ideally be generated under ICL, and any incoming input tax should be carefully evaluated to determine whether it can be reversed and re-claimed under SGL through proper documentation. We would also request you to share an ageing of the input tax balance so that a practical strategy can be developed.

CONCLUSION

In summary, while the merger is legally effective from January 1, 2025, the key focus now is on aligning all tax, operational, and compliance aspects with this position. Immediate actions are required in the areas of withholding tax correction, vendor/customer communication, payroll transition, and sales tax streamlining, while more complex matters such as input tax handling and CPR corrections will require coordinated follow-up with the tax authorities.

We will be pleased to assist you in implementing the above steps and in engaging with the relevant tax offices to ensure a smooth transition.

Best regards,

اسی ایمیل کو تھوڑا سا اور امپروو اگر ایفینیس میں ایریاز ہیں تو اس کو امپروو کر لیں پلس وہ جو ایسٹس آئی سی ایل کے بکس میں پڑے ہوئے ہیں تو وہ زیرو ریٹنگ کی جو انوائس ایشو کرنی ہے وہ تھوڑا سیلز ٹیکس ایکٹ نائنٹی نائنٹی میں دیکھ لیں کہ کیا ہے اور سیکشن کا ریفرنس فگر آؤٹ کریں وہ ذرا سیلز ٹیکس والے جو ہیں اس میں ایک اپروپریٹ ہیڈنگ بنا کے وہ بھی ڈسکس کر لیں اچھا پلس وہ انکم ٹیکس اور سیلز ٹیکس پروفائلز بھی دیکھ لیں کہ جو پریویسز ہیں وہ ساری جو آئی سی ایل کی پریویسلی تھیں وہ ایس جی ایل کے میں آ جائیں ایفینیز اگر فیکٹری پرامٹس وغیرہ ہیں اور جو بھی اس کے رینٹس کے اور جو ویرئس اور کانٹریکٹس ہیں ایگریمنٹس ہیں وہ بھی کسی اپروپریٹ ہیڈنگ بنا کے اور اس کو وہاں سے بھی دیکھ لیں اور کوئی انکم ٹیکس اور سیلز ٹیکس میں کوئی ایسی چیز ہو جس طرح سے کوئی ایسے فیکٹرز ہوں جو یہاں پہ ڈسکس نہیں ہوا تو اس کو بھی دیکھ لیں اور بہت ہی بہت ہی پرائم قسم کی ایک ایمیل بنائیں

In conclusion, the post-merger transition requires a carefully coordinated approach across income tax, sales tax, and operational functions to ensure full alignment with the legal position approved by the Court while minimizing exposure to procedural challenges. Immediate focus should be placed on timely submission of audited accounts, complete migration of tax and commercial activities to SGL, and proactive correction of withholding and sales tax positions. At the same time, given the practical limitations in transferring input tax and tax credits, early engagement with the tax authorities, supported by robust documentation and a clear audit trail, will be essential to safeguard recoverability and avoid future disputes. A disciplined execution of these steps will ensure a smooth transition, preserve tax efficiencies, and maintain a defensible position in the event of any scrutiny.

A more structured and legally aligned position needs to be developed to manage the input tax accumulated in Industrial Clothing Limited (ICL), particularly in light of the merger where Shahbaz Garments Limited (SGL) is the surviving entity.

As you are already aware, despite the business having effectively transitioned to SGL, certain input tax continues to accumulate in ICL. Ideally, from a commercial and tax alignment perspective, this input tax should be available to SGL against its output liability. However, under the current legal and system framework—particularly within the FBR’s IRIS portal—there is no prescribed mechanism that allows a direct transfer of input tax balances from a non-surviving entity to a surviving entity post-merger. We have also previously highlighted that, in practice, the tax authorities have not developed any consistent precedent in this regard. In fact, in similar cases, the department has generally resisted such transfers, often taking technical positions that they are not a party to the merger arrangement or that the law does not expressly permit such adjustments.

In view of these practical limitations, a controlled and forward-looking approach is essential. All future sales tax invoicing must strictly be undertaken under SGL, and no further output tax should be generated under ICL. At the same time, procurement and vendor coordination should be carefully managed to ensure that input tax does not continue to accumulate in ICL. Wherever feasible—particularly for recent transactions falling within the permissible time limits—credit notes may be obtained from suppliers, followed by reissuance of invoices in the name of SGL. This will allow a legitimate shift of input tax to the correct entity without creating exposure.

To effectively evaluate available options, we request you to share a detailed ageing of the input tax balance currently lying in ICL. This will enable us to identify portions that can still be regularized through credit note mechanisms versus those that may require alternative strategies.

In parallel, it would be prudent to formally engage with the concerned Commissioner by way of a written representation, clearly setting out the factual background of the merger and requesting guidance or approval for transfer or adjustment of the accumulated input tax. A meeting with the department should also be arranged to practically explore whether any administrative solution can be worked out, even in the absence of a codified mechanism. This dual approach—operational control along with proactive engagement—will be critical in minimizing potential loss of input tax and managing the position defensibly.

You are right to specifically refer to Section 61(4) of the entity["law","Income Tax Ordinance, 2001","Pakistan tax law"], as this sub-section is the decisive provision on this point.

Section 61(4) clearly provides that **no tax credit shall be allowed in respect of any donation unless the payment is made through a crossed cheque, bank draft, pay order, or any other banking channel as prescribed**. The intent of the law is to ensure traceability and proper documentation of the donation.

From a practical compliance perspective, this means that **cash donations—irrespective of supporting receipts—do not qualify for tax credit**. In assessments and payroll reviews, the tax authorities strictly rely on the mode of payment, not merely the acknowledgment issued by the donee organization.

Accordingly, your position remains fully aligned with the law:  
the employee’s claim based on cash donation/Zakat receipts is not admissible for tax credit purposes.

Yes, your understanding is correct. Under the provisions of the entity["law","Income Tax Ordinance, 2001","Pakistan tax law"], tax credit in respect of donations (including Zakat) is governed by Section 61, which clearly requires that the donation must be made through **verifiable banking channels**. Cash donations do not fulfill this condition, as they cannot be independently traced or substantiated through the prescribed mode of payment.

In practical terms, even if an employee provides a cash receipt from a charitable organization, such payment does not qualify for tax credit in the salary computation because the law places emphasis on **mode of payment rather than merely the existence of a receipt**. The Federal Board of Revenue has consistently taken this position during assessments, and such claims are typically disallowed where payment is made in cash.

Accordingly, the employee’s request for tax credit against cash donations/Zakat cannot be entertained for payroll tax purposes. You may advise the employee that only donations made through crossed cheque, bank transfer, or other documented banking instruments—paid to an approved donee—are eligible for tax credit under the law.

In particular, Section 61(4) explicitly requires that the donation must be made through **recognized banking channels**—such as crossed cheque, bank draft, pay order, or other prescribed modes—for the tax credit to be admissible.  

Accordingly, donations made in cash do not meet this statutory requirement, even if supported by receipts issued by the recipient organization. The law places primary reliance on the **mode of payment and its traceability**, and therefore such cash contributions are not eligible for tax credit in the salary computation.  

In view of the above, the employee’s request for claiming tax credit against cash donation/Zakat receipts cannot be accommodated. You may advise the employee that only donations made through proper banking channels to eligible institutions would qualify for tax credit under the applicable provisions.

جی، سرچ کے بعد **relevant material ملا ہے** جس سے یہ position support ہوتی ہے کہ **export cargo / export containers کو Rule 40 میں expressly taxable service کے طور پر بعد میں include کیا گیا**۔

اہم finding یہ ہے کہ SRB Rules میں پہلے Rule 40 کے تحت port/terminal operator کی services **import cargo، transit cargo، اور transshipment cargo** کے حوالے سے taxable لکھی ہوئی تھیں۔ بعد میں SRB نے Finance Act / Notifications 2020 کے ذریعے یہ change کیا کہ **“service provided in relation to cargo exported shall also be included in taxable service.”** citeturn375559search2turn375559search5

اس کا practical implication یہ بنتا ہے کہ **1 July 2020 سے پہلے export cargo / export containers کے حوالے سے terminal operator services کی taxability expressly Rule 40 میں شامل نہیں تھی**؛ یعنی ہمارے argument کے لیے یہ material useful ہے کہ export containers پر SST کی applicability subsequent amendment کے ذریعے bring-in کی گئی، اس لیے earlier periods کے لیے department کا retrospective demand بنانا contestable ہے۔ Tola Associates کے June 2020 update میں بھی یہی لکھا ہے کہ Rule 40 میں پہلے imported / transit / transshipment cargo تھا، اور “now” export cargo کو بھی include کیا گیا۔ citeturn834740search1

Official SRB search results میں terminal operator کی definition بھی ملتی ہے، جس میں KICT, PICT اور QICT وغیرہ شامل ہیں؛ اس لیے یہ material container terminals پر directly relevant ہے۔ citeturn710894search5

میری view میں اس کو reply/appeal میں اس طرح use کیا جا سکتا ہے: **“The subsequent inclusion of services in relation to exported cargo under Rule 40 itself demonstrates that, prior to such amendment, the rule did not expressly cover export cargo/export containers. Therefore, any attempt to levy SST on export containers for the earlier period would amount to retrospective application of a later amendment, which is not permissible unless expressly provided by law.”**

Yes, based on a detailed review of available material, there is **supportive basis to argue that services relating to export containers were not originally covered under SRB’s taxable scope for terminal operators and were brought into the net later through an amendment**.

The key development arises under **Rule 40 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Rules, 2011**, which governs taxation of port and terminal operator services. Initially, the rule specifically covered services in relation to **import cargo, transit cargo, and transshipment cargo**. However, through amendments introduced around **2020 (via Finance Act / SRB notifications)**, the scope was expanded to expressly include **“services provided in relation to cargo exported.”**

This is not merely a clarification but a **substantive expansion of scope**, and that distinction is critical. The fact that export cargo had to be specifically inserted later indicates that **prior to such amendment, export-related services (including export containers handled by terminal operators) were not explicitly taxable under Rule 40**.

From a litigation standpoint, this creates a strong and practical argument:

In earlier periods (i.e., pre-amendment), any attempt by the department to levy Sindh Sales Tax on services relating to export containers can be challenged on the basis that:
- The charging framework did not expressly cover export cargo;
- Tax statutes must be interpreted strictly, and nothing can be implied;
- A subsequent amendment cannot be applied retrospectively unless clearly stated in law.

In practical terms, this argument has been successfully raised in similar port/terminal cases where the department tried to **extend the scope of Rule 40 beyond its original wording**.

If you are building a reply or appeal, the position can be framed along these lines:

> “The subsequent inclusion of ‘export cargo’ within Rule 40 clearly demonstrates that, prior to such amendment, services in relation to export containers were not within the taxable ambit. Therefore, any demand raised for periods preceding the amendment constitutes an impermissible retrospective application of law.”

If you want, I can further align this specifically with your **PICT / FTS / wharfage position** and draft a litigation-ready paragraph with case-law style backing.

---

## 1. **Qasim International Container Terminal Case (Leading Case)**  
**entity["legal_case","Qasim International Container Terminal Pakistan Ltd. v. Federation of Pakistan","2020 PTD 1952 Sindh High Court"]**

یہ ایک **Division Bench judgment** ہے جس کو بعد میں بھی High Court نے follow کیا (2025 کے order میں بھی confirm ہوا)۔ citeturn0search7  

### Key relevance (آپ کے case کے لیے):
- یہ case container terminal operators (QICT) کے tax / regulatory disputes سے متعلق ہے  
- Court نے واضح کیا کہ:
  - terminal operators کی activities کو mechanically tax نہیں کیا جا سکتا  
  - legal framework اور specific charging provisions دیکھنے پڑتے ہیں  
- 2025 کے order میں بھی کہا گیا کہ subsequent petitions **“squarely covered”** ہیں اس judgment سے  

👉 Practical use:  
یہ آپ کو یہ argument دینے میں help کرتا ہے کہ  
**terminal operator services کو broad interpretation دے کر tax impose نہیں کیا جا سکتا — بلکہ express legal coverage ضروری ہے۔**

---

## 2. **High Court Order – Container Terminal Operations (Port Qasim case)**  
**entity["legal_case","Suit No. 1414 of 2019 (Off Dock Terminal vs Container Terminal Operator)","Sindh High Court Karachi"]**

citeturn0search0  

### Key findings:
- Court نے واضح کیا کہ:
  - container terminal operator کا role صرف **handling / service provision** ہے  
  - وہ cargo (including export cargo) کو refuse نہیں کر سکتا  
- Court نے کہا:
  > operator cannot refuse handling of containers; they only charge for services  

👉 Practical implication:
- یہ establish کرتا ہے کہ terminal operator کی nature **pure service provider** ہے  
- یعنی taxability بھی **service nature اور statutory coverage** پر depend کرے گی، نہ کہ cargo movement پر  

---

## 3. **Indirect but Strong Inference (آپ کے core point کے لیے)**

ان دونوں cases کو combine کریں تو ایک strong litigation position بنتی ہے:

### (A) Courts نے کیا کہا:
- terminal operators = service providers  
- taxation requires **clear legal basis**  
- broad یا implied interpretation acceptable نہیں  

### (B) Rule 40 amendment (آپ نے جو پہلے identify کیا):
- export cargo later include ہوا  

### (C) Combined argument:
> اگر terminal operator services پہلے ہی export cargo پر taxable ہوتی تو Rule 40 میں بعد میں insertion کی ضرورت ہی نہیں تھی  

---

## 4. Litigation-ready positioning (آپ کے style میں)

آپ اس کو appeal / reply میں اس طرح frame کر سکتے ہیں:

> “It is respectfully submitted that the legal position governing container terminal operators has been examined by the Honorable Sindh High Court in the case of Qasim International Container Terminal Pakistan Ltd. (2020 PTD 1952), wherein it has been held that taxation of terminal operator services must strictly flow from the charging provisions and cannot be assumed on a presumptive or extended basis.  
>  
> Furthermore, judicial observations in port-related disputes have consistently recognized that terminal operators merely render handling services and do not independently alter the nature of cargo, whether import or export.  
>  
> In this backdrop, the subsequent inclusion of ‘export cargo’ within Rule 40 clearly evidences that prior to such amendment, services in relation to export containers were not within the taxable ambit. Any attempt to levy tax for earlier periods would therefore amount to an impermissible retrospective application of law.”

---

## Bottom line (straight professional view)

- Direct SRB-specific فیصلہ export containers پر شاید limited ہو  
- لیکن:
  - **QICT judgment (2020 PTD 1952)**  
  - **Port Qasim terminal handling case (SHC)**  
➡️ دونوں ملا کر **strong legal framework provide کرتے ہیں**  

یہ exactly وہ type کا material ہے جو Tribunal / Commissioner Appeals میں weight رکھتا ہے — especially جب آپ Rule 40 amendment کے ساتھ combine کریں۔

---

اگر آپ چاہیں تو میں specifically **PICT / wharfage / FTS reconciliation کے ساتھ fully drafted grounds of appeal** بھی تیار کر دیتا ہوں — وہ اور بھی زیادہ powerful بن جائے گا۔

Lastly, the **maximum cap of 200% of tax payable** should also be tested, particularly in cases where tax liability is low but delay is significant.

Based on our discussion and our earlier detailed advice on similar upstream sector transactions, we have set out below a refined and logical analysis of the two restructuring options considered, namely (i) cross-border merger and (ii) form-in / form-out structure.

Starting with the cross-border merger option, while such mergers may be legally possible depending on the laws of the relevant jurisdictions, the key issue from a Pakistan tax perspective is that this route does not qualify as a tax-neutral event. Under Section 97A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, tax neutrality is only available where both merging entities are companies incorporated in Pakistan. In the present case, since the existing presence is through branches of foreign companies, this condition is not met. Therefore, even if a merger is achieved at a legal level, it will not be recognized as a tax-neutral merger in Pakistan.

As a result, the transaction is likely to be treated as a disposal of assets or business interests situated in Pakistan. In this regard, Sections 101(9) and 101(10) clearly provide that any gain arising from the alienation of rights to explore or exploit natural resources in Pakistan, or shares deriving value from such rights, is treated as Pakistan-source income fileciteturn0file0. This means that even if the transaction is executed outside Pakistan, the gain remains taxable in Pakistan.

In addition, Section 101A introduces a mechanism to capture indirect disposals, under which the buyer may be required to withhold tax (generally 10% of the fair market value). In practice, we have seen that even where the legal position is arguable, regulatory approvals are often linked with payment of this tax fileciteturn0file2. Therefore, from a practical standpoint, this exposure cannot be avoided.

It is also important to consider recent treaty changes. Under the updated provisions (post MLI), where shares derive more than 50% of their value from immovable property or natural resources in Pakistan, the right to tax such gains shifts to Pakistan. Since upstream assets fall within this definition, treaty protection is generally no longer available in such cases fileciteturn0file1.

Another important aspect is valuation. Under Section 77, tax is applied on the higher of the actual consideration or fair market value (FMV). This creates risk not only for the seller but also for the buyer, as the tax authorities may challenge the valuation and apply adjustments accordingly fileciteturn0file0. In upstream transactions, valuation of reserves and working interest is often subjective and closely scrutinized.

Further, even where the transaction is structured as a share sale, the tax authorities have consistently taken the position that such transactions effectively represent disposal of working interest and have taxed them under Section 39 as “Income from Other Sources” at full rates. This position has been followed in recent cases and is difficult to challenge in practice fileciteturn0file0.

In light of the above, the cross-border merger option, while legally possible, does not provide any tax advantage in Pakistan and is likely to result in immediate tax exposure.

Moving to the form-in / form-out option, this involves setting up a local company in Pakistan, transferring the business or working interest into that entity (form-in), and subsequently closing the existing branch structures (form-out). From an implementation perspective, this is generally more straightforward and gives better control over operations going forward.

However, from a tax perspective, this also does not result in a tax-neutral outcome. The transfer of working interest or business into the new company will be treated as a taxable event. Based on our earlier advice and consistent departmental practice, such gains are typically taxed under Section 39 as “Income from Other Sources,” rather than under Section 37 as capital gains fileciteturn0file0. Accordingly, the full corporate tax rate would apply.

The gain in this case would be computed based on the difference between the transfer value (or FMV under Section 77, if higher) and the cost attributable to Pakistan operations. It is important to note that only direct costs relating to the acquisition and development of the working interest are generally allowed, while broader overheads are not accepted.

One advantage of this structure is that the new local entity may be able to claim amortization of the acquired working interest as an intangible asset under Section 24, provided the transaction is properly structured and tax is discharged by the seller. This can provide tax relief over time at the level of the new entity.

Finally, in both options, it is important to highlight that accumulated tax losses at the branch level cannot be carried forward or transferred. Since the conditions of Section 97A are not met, there is no mechanism to preserve these losses post-restructuring. Accordingly, such losses will remain within the existing structures and will effectively lapse upon closure.

To summarize in simple terms, both options lead to taxation in Pakistan. The cross-border merger does not achieve tax neutrality and involves additional complexity from a regulatory and treaty perspective. The form-in / form-out option is relatively more practical to implement and provides a cleaner structure going forward, although it also results in upfront tax on transfer. The decision, therefore, should be based on commercial priorities, ease of execution, and overall cost impact rather than expectation of tax neutrality.

We would be happy to discuss this further and assist in evaluating the most suitable approach based on your specific group structure.

Please feel free to reach out in case of any clarification.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
TAX WAY
:::

I have carefully reviewed all three documents you shared. Below is a structured and practical synthesis of the key tax positions, strictly based on those documents, without adding any external assumptions:

---

## 1. Core Tax Principle – Pakistan Taxability

Across all documents, the position is consistent and quite firm:

- **Any gain on disposal of:**
  - shares of a company (even foreign), **or**
  - working interest in petroleum concessions in Pakistan  

  **is taxable in Pakistan** under Sections **101(9) and 101(10)**. fileciteturn0file0

- This applies **even if:**
  - transaction is executed offshore  
  - parties are non-residents  
  - consideration is paid outside Pakistan  

👉 Practically, this means the **source rule overrides location of transaction or payment**.

---

## 2. Nature of Income – Critical Practical Reality

Although technically:

- Share sale → **Capital Gains (Section 37)**
- Working interest → **Income from Other Sources (Section 39)**

However, in **actual practice:**

- Tax authorities **consistently treat both** (including share sales) as:
  > **“Income from Other Sources” under Section 39**  
  taxed at **full corporate rate (~29%)** fileciteturn0file0

👉 Even where capital gain treatment is arguable, **departmental position prevails in almost all recent cases**.

---

## 3. Treaty Position – Now Significantly Restricted

Earlier:

- Pakistan–Netherlands treaty could exempt gains on share disposal.

Now (post MLI modification):

- If shares derive **>50% value from immovable property/natural resources in Pakistan**,  
  → **Pakistan gets taxing rights** fileciteturn0file1

- “Immovable property” explicitly includes:
  - rights to explore/exploit natural resources

👉 Result:
- **Treaty protection is no longer available in such cases.**

---

## 4. Finance Act Changes – Important Impact

Two key updates:

### (a) Capital Gains Relief Removed
- 25% reduction for assets held >1 year **abolished (from July 1, 2022)** fileciteturn0file1  
👉 Now:
- Entire gain taxed at full rate

---

### (b) Withholding on Share Transfers Introduced
- Buyer must withhold:
  - **10% of FMV of shares** fileciteturn0file1  

- FMV determined under **Rule 19H**

👉 Important:
- This is **advance tax**, not final
- Seller still files return and determines actual liability

---

## 5. Fair Market Value (FMV) Risk

Very critical exposure highlighted:

- Tax applies on:
  > **Higher of consideration OR FMV** fileciteturn0file0  

- Both parties may face tax:
  - Seller → on gain  
  - Buyer → under unexplained investment (Section 111)

👉 Practical implication:
- **Valuation is the most sensitive area in these transactions**

---

## 6. Working Interest vs Share Sale – Strategic Difference

### Sale of Shares:
- Possible structuring route
- But:
  - taxed in Pakistan
  - treaty protection largely ineffective
  - recharacterisation risk

---

### Sale of Working Interest:
- Clearly taxable in Pakistan
- No treaty protection
- Treated as:
  > **Income from Other Sources (Section 39)** fileciteturn0file0  

- Buyer benefit:
  - amortization of intangible allowed (Section 24)

👉 Practical takeaway:
- From FBR’s perspective, **both routes lead to taxation**

---

## 7. Withholding Tax Mechanism

### Share Sale:
- Section 101A / Section 37 mechanism:
  - Buyer withholds **10% of FMV**

- Even where technically not applicable (non-resident buyer):
  - **FBR still enforces payment via approval conditions** fileciteturn0file2  

---

### Working Interest:
- Generally:
  - withholding may not apply between non-residents  
- BUT:
  - if payer has Pakistan presence → **Section 152 applies**

👉 In practice:
- **FBR ensures tax collection before granting transaction approvals**

---

## 8. Super Tax Exposure

- Applicable if income exceeds threshold (Rs 150 million)  
- Includes capital gains  
fileciteturn0file2  

👉 So large disposals **will trigger Super Tax under Section 4C**

---

## 9. Regulatory & Compliance Reality

From practical experience noted in documents:

- Sellers must:
  - register with FBR
  - file return in Pakistan  
fileciteturn0file2  

- Even non-residents:
  - cannot avoid compliance

- In some cases:
  - tax paid without registration (not recommended)

👉 Also:
- Government approvals (DGPC, etc.) are often:
  > **conditional upon tax payment**

---

## 10. Key Commercial Risks Identified

The documents repeatedly highlight real-world risks:

- Treaty benefits **not honored by FBR**
- Transactions **recharacterised**
- FMV disputes
- Double taxation (seller + buyer)
- Withholding forced even where not legally clear
- Litigation takes years (High Court cases pending)

---

## 11. Overall Practical Conclusion

Based strictly on the documents:

- **Pakistan has a very aggressive and substance-over-form approach** for such transactions.
- Structuring (shares vs working interest) **does not eliminate tax exposure**.
- Treaty reliance is **no longer viable in petroleum/natural resource cases**.
- **Tax payment is effectively unavoidable** to complete transactions and obtain approvals.
- Valuation and documentation (especially SPA and independent valuation) are **critical risk areas**.

---

If you want, I can now convert this into:
- a formal advisory memo, or  
- a deal structuring note highlighting optimal approach and risk mitigation  

based on these exact positions.

:::writing{variant="email" id="84271" subject="High-Level Tax Considerations – Restructuring Options for Renter Energy Group"}
Dear [Client Name],

We hope you are doing well.

Further to our recent discussion with the Renter Energy team, we understand that various entities within the Renter Energy Group are currently operating in Pakistan through branch structures across multiple jurisdictions. As highlighted during the meeting, this has resulted in increased compliance requirements and duplication of efforts, prompting consideration of a restructuring exercise to streamline operations.

As requested, we set out below our high-level comments on the two possible restructuring options discussed, namely (i) cross-border merger, and (ii) form-in / form-out structure.

From a cross-border merger perspective, while such mergers may be feasible from a corporate law standpoint depending on the legal framework of the respective jurisdictions involved, the key limitation from a Pakistan tax perspective is that such a restructuring would not qualify as a tax-neutral event. Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, tax neutrality for mergers is governed by Section 97A, which specifically applies to mergers of locally incorporated companies. Since branches operating in Pakistan do not constitute locally incorporated entities, the benefit of tax neutrality would not be available in this case. Accordingly, any consolidation or merger of branch operations, even if achieved through a cross-border legal mechanism, may be treated as a taxable disposal of assets and business interests in Pakistan. 

Furthermore, recent judicial developments have reinforced the position that tax-neutral merger provisions are to be strictly interpreted and are not extendable to structures involving foreign entities or branches. In addition, such restructuring may also trigger implications under indirect disposal provisions (including Section 101A), particularly where underlying assets in Pakistan derive substantial value from local operations. Therefore, even where the transaction is executed offshore, the Pakistan tax exposure may still arise. These aspects would need to be carefully evaluated in light of the specific jurisdictions involved and applicable regulatory approvals.

On the other hand, the form-in / form-out mechanism appears to be a relatively more practical route from an implementation perspective. This would typically involve incorporating a local entity, transferring the business / working interest into such entity (form-in), followed by closure or exit of the existing branch structures (form-out). However, it is important to note that this route also does not result in a tax-neutral outcome. The transfer of business or working interest would generally be treated as a taxable event, akin to a disposal, and corresponding tax implications would arise in Pakistan. 

In this context, the tax treatment would largely align with principles applicable to transfer of working interest, including potential exposure under “income from other sources” and valuation considerations based on fair market value. While this option may provide operational and compliance efficiencies going forward, the upfront tax cost would need to be evaluated and factored into the overall restructuring decision.

In both scenarios discussed above, it is important to highlight that any accumulated tax losses at the branch level would not be available for carry forward or utilization post-restructuring. The tax loss regime under Pakistani law is entity-specific and does not generally permit transfer of losses in cases where tax-neutral merger provisions are not applicable. Accordingly, such losses would remain stranded within the existing structures and would lapse upon closure or restructuring.

In summary, while both options are legally and commercially viable subject to further detailed evaluation, neither route provides a tax-neutral outcome in Pakistan. The choice between the two would therefore need to be driven by a balance between commercial objectives, regulatory feasibility, and overall tax cost.

We would be pleased to discuss these options further and perform a more detailed analysis based on the specific group structure and jurisdictions involved.

Please feel free to reach out in case of any clarification.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
TAX WAY

In this regard, sections 101(9) and 101(10) clearly provide that any gain arising from the alienation of rights to explore or exploit natural resources in Pakistan, or shares deriving value from such rights, is treated as Pakistan-source income. This means that even if the transaction is executed outside Pakistan, the gain remains taxable in Pakistan.
In addition, section 101A introduces a mechanism to capture indirect disposals, under which the buyer may be required to withhold tax (generally 10% of the fair market value). In practice, we have seen that even where the legal position is arguable, regulatory approvals are often linked with payment of this tax. Therefore, from a practical standpoint, this exposure cannot be avoided.
It is also important to consider recent treaty changes. Under the updated provisions (post MLI), where shares derive more than 50% of their value from immovable property or natural resources in Pakistan, the right to tax such gains shifts to Pakistan. Since upstream assets fall within this definition, treaty protection is generally no longer available in such cases.
Another important aspect is valuation. Under section 77, tax is applied on the higher of the actual consideration or fair market value (FMV). This creates risk not only for the seller but also for the buyer, as the tax authorities may challenge the valuation and apply adjustments accordingly. In upstream transactions, valuation of reserves and working interest is often subjective and closely scrutinized.
Further, even where the transaction is structured as a share sale, the tax authorities have consistently taken the position that such transactions effectively represent disposal of working interest and have taxed them under section 39 as ‘Income from Other Sources’ at full rates. This position has been followed in recent cases and is difficult to challenge in practice.
In light of the above, the cross-border merger option, without prejudice to legally possible, does not provide any tax advantage in Pakistan and is likely to result in immediate tax exposure.
Moving to the form-in / form-out option, transferring the business or working interest into that entity (form-in), and subsequently closing the existing branch structures (form-out). From an implementation perspective, this is generally more straightforward and gives better control over operations going forward.
However, from a tax perspective, this also does not result in a tax-neutral outcome. The transfer of working interest or business into the new company will be treated as a taxable event. Based on our experience and consistent departmental practice, such gains are typically taxed under section 39 as ‘Income from Other Sources,’ rather than under section 37 as capital gains. Accordingly, the full corporate tax rate would apply.
The gain in this case would be computed based on the difference between the transfer value (or FMV under Section 77, if higher) and the cost attributable to operations. It is important to note that only direct costs relating to the acquisition and development of the working interest are generally allowed, while broader overheads are not accepted.
One advantage of this structure is that the new local entity may be able to claim amortization of the acquired working interest as an intangible asset under section 24. This can provide tax relief over time at the level of the entity.
Finally, in both options, it is important to highlight that accumulated tax losses at the branch level cannot be carried forward or transferred. Since the conditions of section 97A are not met, there is no mechanism to preserve these losses post-restructuring. Accordingly, such losses will remain within the existing structures and will effectively lapse upon closure.
To summarize in simple terms, both options lead to taxation in Pakistan. The cross-border merger does not achieve tax neutrality and involves additional complexity from a regulatory and treaty perspective. The form-in / form-out option is relatively more practical to implement and provides a cleaner structure going forward, although it also results in upfront tax on transfer. The decision, therefore, should be based on commercial priorities, ease of execution, and overall cost impact rather than expectation of tax neutrality.
We would be happy to discuss this further and assist in evaluating the most suitable approach based on your specific group structure.
Please feel free to reach out in case of any clarification.
Best regards,

Dear [Client Name],

We hope you are doing well.

Further to our recent meeting with the United Energy team, we understand that multiple entities within the United Energy Group, incorporated across various jurisdictions, are currently operating in Pakistan through branch structures. As discussed, this has resulted in significant compliance overlap, duplication of reporting, and administrative inefficiencies. In this context, you had requested our detailed views on potential restructuring options to streamline the Pakistan operations.

Based on our discussion and drawing upon our earlier detailed advice on similar upstream sector transactions, we set out below a comprehensive analysis of the two restructuring options considered, namely (i) cross-border merger, and (ii) form-in / form-out mechanism.

From a cross-border merger perspective, while such restructuring may be achievable from a legal standpoint subject to the corporate laws of the respective jurisdictions, the Pakistan tax implications remain a key constraint. Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, tax neutrality for mergers is specifically governed by Section 97A, which applies only where both merging entities are companies incorporated in Pakistan. In the present case, since the existing presence in Pakistan is through branches of foreign companies, the conditions prescribed under Section 97A are not met. Accordingly, any merger—even if legally recognized offshore—would not qualify as a tax-neutral reorganization for Pakistan tax purposes.

In practical terms, such a restructuring is likely to be treated as a disposal of underlying assets and business interests situated in Pakistan. In this regard, Sections 101(9) and 101(10) become particularly relevant, which deem gains arising from alienation of any right to explore or exploit natural resources in Pakistan, or shares deriving their value wholly or principally from such rights, as Pakistan-source income. As also noted in our earlier advice, the tax authorities have consistently invoked these provisions to tax offshore transactions involving indirect disposal of Pakistan assets, irrespective of the location of execution or receipt of consideration fileciteturn0file0.

Further, Section 101A introduces a withholding mechanism on indirect disposals, whereby the buyer is required to withhold tax—generally at 10% of the fair market value (FMV)—on acquisition of shares deriving value from Pakistan assets. Even in cases involving non-resident buyers, it has been observed that regulatory approvals (including those from DGPC/FBR) are often made conditional upon payment of such tax fileciteturn0file2. Accordingly, the practical enforceability of this provision cannot be ignored.

It is also important to highlight that, following amendments to international tax treaties (particularly post-MLI changes), the availability of treaty protection has been significantly curtailed. Where shares derive more than 50% of their value from immovable property or natural resources in Pakistan, taxing rights are now allocated to Pakistan, thereby limiting the ability to claim exemption under treaties fileciteturn0file1.

In addition, any such restructuring would be subject to valuation considerations under Section 77, whereby the transaction is taxed based on the higher of consideration received or FMV. This creates exposure not only for the seller but also for the buyer under Section 111(3), potentially resulting in dual taxation on valuation differences fileciteturn0file0. Given the nature of upstream assets, valuation of reserves and working interest remains a highly sensitive and frequently litigated area.

Separately, there is also a strong likelihood that even where a share sale structure is adopted, the tax authorities may recharacterize the transaction as disposal of working interest and tax the same under Section 39 as “Income from Other Sources,” taxable at the full corporate rate. This position has consistently been taken in recent transactions and upheld in appellate proceedings fileciteturn0file0.

In light of the above, while cross-border merger may appear feasible from a legal structuring standpoint, it does not provide a tax-efficient outcome in Pakistan and is likely to trigger immediate tax costs.

Turning to the form-in / form-out option, this mechanism involves incorporation of a local entity in Pakistan (form-in), transfer of business / working interest into such entity, followed by closure or exit of the existing branch structures (form-out). From an implementation perspective, this is generally considered a more straightforward route; however, the tax implications remain broadly similar in principle.

The transfer of working interest or business from branch to a newly incorporated entity would constitute a taxable event. As per established positions under the Ordinance and consistent with prior transaction precedents, such gains are typically taxed under Section 39 as “Income from Other Sources,” particularly where the consideration relates to rights to explore or exploit natural resources. Although an argument may exist to treat such gains under Section 37 as capital gains, the tax authorities have consistently rejected this treatment and taxed such income at normal rates under Section 39 fileciteturn0file0.

From a computational standpoint, the gain would be determined as the difference between sale consideration (or FMV under Section 77, if higher) and the cost of acquisition attributable to Pakistan operations. It is pertinent to note that only Pakistan-specific costs relating to acquisition and development of the working interest are generally allowed, and broader group-level costs are typically disallowed.

An important commercial consideration in favour of this structure is that the buyer (i.e., the newly incorporated entity) may be eligible to claim amortization of intangible assets under Section 24, where the seller has discharged tax on the transfer under Section 39. This has been allowed in certain past cases and may provide future tax benefits to the local entity.

However, it must be emphasized that neither the cross-border merger nor the form-in / form-out option allows for preservation or utilization of accumulated tax losses at the branch level. Since Section 97A is not applicable, there is no mechanism under the law to transfer such losses to another entity. Accordingly, any carried forward losses would remain stranded and would lapse upon closure of the existing branch structures.

In summary, based on the current legal framework and practical enforcement trends:

- Cross-border merger does not qualify as a tax-neutral event under Section 97A and is likely to trigger taxation under Sections 101 and 101A, along with associated valuation and withholding implications.  
- Form-in / form-out, while operationally more practical, also results in a taxable transfer of working interest, generally taxed under Section 39 at full rates, albeit with potential downstream benefits in terms of amortization.  
- Treaty protection is largely unavailable in the present context due to recent amendments and the nature of underlying assets.  
- Accumulated tax losses will not be available post-restructuring under either option.  

We would be pleased to further refine this analysis based on the specific jurisdictions involved and assist in evaluating the most optimal structure from a commercial and tax perspective.

Please feel free to reach out in case of any clarification.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
TAX WAY

:::writing{variant="email" id="68125" subject="Restructuring Options – United Energy Group (Pakistan Branch Operations)"}
Dear Sir,

We hope you are doing well.

**Background and Objective**  
Further to our recent discussion, we understand that various entities within the United Energy Group, incorporated across different jurisdictions, are operating in Pakistan through branch structures. This has resulted in duplication of compliance requirements, multiple filings, and operational inefficiencies. You had requested us to outline a practical and tax-efficient way forward to streamline these operations.

Based on our discussion and our earlier experience on similar upstream sector transactions, we have set out below two possible restructuring options, namely (i) cross-border merger and (ii) form-in / form-out structure, along with their key tax implications.

---

**Option 1: Cross-Border Merger – Overview**  
From a legal standpoint, cross-border mergers may be possible depending on the laws of the relevant jurisdictions. However, from a Pakistan tax perspective, this route does not qualify as a tax-neutral event.

---

**Tax Neutrality – Section 97A Limitation**  
Under Section 97A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, tax neutrality is only available where both merging entities are companies incorporated in Pakistan. In the present case, since the operations are carried out through branches of foreign companies, this condition is not met. Accordingly, even if a merger is achieved at a group level, it will not be recognized as a tax-neutral merger in Pakistan.

---

**Taxability of Underlying Assets – Sections 101(9) & 101(10)**  
As a result, the transaction is likely to be treated as a disposal of assets or business interests situated in Pakistan. Sections 101(9) and 101(10) clearly provide that any gain arising from the alienation of rights to explore or exploit natural resources in Pakistan, or shares deriving value from such rights, is treated as Pakistan-source income. This position applies irrespective of where the transaction is executed.

---

**Indirect Disposal & Withholding – Section 101A**  
Section 101A introduces a mechanism to capture indirect disposals, whereby the buyer may be required to withhold tax (generally 10% of the fair market value). In practice, even where the legal position is arguable, regulatory approvals are often linked with payment of this tax. Therefore, this exposure needs to be considered as a practical cost.

---

**Treaty Position – Post MLI Impact**  
Following recent treaty amendments (post MLI), where shares derive more than 50% of their value from immovable property or natural resources in Pakistan, taxing rights shift to Pakistan. Given the nature of upstream assets, treaty protection is generally not available in such cases.

---

**Valuation Exposure – Section 77**  
Another important aspect is valuation. Under Section 77, tax is applied on the higher of the actual consideration or fair market value (FMV). This creates exposure for both seller and buyer, particularly in upstream transactions where valuation of reserves and working interest is subjective and closely scrutinized.

---

**Characterization Risk – Section 39 vs Section 37**  
Even where the transaction is structured as a share sale, the tax authorities have consistently taken the position that such transactions effectively represent disposal of working interest and have taxed them under Section 39 as “Income from Other Sources,” instead of Section 37 (capital gains). This results in taxation at full corporate rates and has been difficult to challenge in practice.

---

**Conclusion – Cross-Border Merger**  
In summary, while legally possible, the cross-border merger option does not provide any tax advantage in Pakistan and is likely to result in immediate tax exposure along with valuation and withholding risks.

---

**Option 2: Form-In / Form-Out – Overview**  
Under this structure, a local company is incorporated in Pakistan (form-in), the business or working interest is transferred into that entity, and the existing branch structures are subsequently closed (form-out). From an operational perspective, this is generally more straightforward and provides better long-term control.

---

**Tax Treatment of Transfer – Section 39**  
From a tax perspective, this transfer will also be treated as a taxable event. Based on consistent departmental practice, gains arising on transfer of working interest are typically taxed under Section 39 as “Income from Other Sources,” rather than under Section 37 as capital gains. Accordingly, the full corporate tax rate would apply.

---

**Computation of Gain – Section 77 Principles**  
The gain would be computed as the difference between the transfer value (or FMV under Section 77, if higher) and the cost attributable to Pakistan operations. It is important to note that only direct costs relating to acquisition and development are generally allowed, while overheads are typically disallowed.

---

**Future Tax Benefit – Section 24 (Amortization)**  
One advantage of this structure is that the new local entity may be able to claim amortization of the acquired working interest as an intangible asset under Section 24. This provides a tax benefit over time and partially offsets the upfront tax cost.

---

**Tax Losses – Non-Availability Post Restructuring**  
In both options, accumulated tax losses at the branch level cannot be carried forward or transferred. Since the conditions of Section 97A are not met, there is no mechanism to preserve these losses. Accordingly, such losses will remain stranded and lapse upon closure of the branches.

---

**Overall Summary and Way Forward**  
In simple terms, both options result in taxation in Pakistan. The cross-border merger involves higher complexity with no tax neutrality and additional treaty and withholding issues. The form-in / form-out option, while also taxable, is relatively more practical to implement and provides a cleaner operational structure along with future amortization benefits.

Accordingly, the decision should be driven by commercial objectives, ease of execution, and overall tax cost, rather than expectation of tax neutrality.

We would be pleased to discuss this further and assist in evaluating the most suitable approach based on your detailed group structure.

Please feel free to reach out in case of any clarification.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
TAX WAY

The Pakistan Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), through SRO No. 55(I)/2025 dated 24 January 2025, has introduced significant changes to the monthly sales tax return form. These changes require all registered manufacturers, commercial importers, distributors and wholesalers supplying taxable goods to provide on the return both the value and quantity of the goods produced, acquired and sold.

In the absence of a specific effective date, the changes likely take effect immediately and will be applicable to sales tax returns filed for January 2025 and thereafter.

Key Changes
Submission of "Annexure — J" by manufacturers
All registered manufacturers supplying taxable goods are now required to submit, with their monthly sales tax return, "Annexure — J," which was previously required only for specific sectors. The required information includes the description of goods (HS Code, Unit of Measurement), the value of opening stock, goods manufactured and supplied during the tax period and closing stock along with their quantities.

Submission of "Annexure - H1" by importers and distributors
Registered commercial importers, distributors and wholesalers supplying taxable goods are now required to provide itemized/product-wise (HS code-based) quantity and stock details in the newly introduced Annexure - H1 form, along with their monthly sales tax return. All information required in Annexure - H1 will be based on the cost or purchase price of the registered person.

Compliance implications
Filing the Annexures J and H1 will be mandatory, starting with the January 2025 sales tax return.

Of key importance immediately will be determining the closing stock as of 31 December 2024, which can then be declared as the opening stock in the January 2025 sales tax return.

The Pakistan Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), through S.R.O. 55(I)/2025 dated January 24, 2025, has introduced significant revisions to the monthly sales tax return format, fundamentally enhancing the level of transactional and inventory-based disclosures required from registered persons. Under the revised framework, all registered manufacturers, commercial importers, distributors, and wholesalers engaged in the supply of taxable goods are now required to report both the **value and quantitative details** of goods produced, acquired, and supplied during the tax period. In the absence of a specifically notified effective date, these changes are generally understood to be applicable from the January 2025 tax period onwards, thereby impacting returns filed thereafter.

A key structural change introduced through the aforesaid S.R.O. is the mandatory submission of **Annexure J** by manufacturers. Previously limited in scope to certain sectors, Annexure J now requires all manufacturers supplying taxable goods to furnish detailed stock and production information as part of their monthly return. This includes disclosure of goods on an item-wise basis, supported by HS codes and units of measurement, along with values and quantities of opening stock, goods manufactured, goods supplied during the period, and closing stock. The intent is clearly to establish a complete audit trail of inventory movements within the manufacturing cycle, aligned strictly with taxable supplies.

Similarly, the introduction of **Annexure H-1** imposes comparable reporting obligations on commercial importers, distributors, and wholesalers. These categories of taxpayers are now required to submit product-wise, HS code-based details of stock and transactions, including quantities and values, based on cost or purchase price. This annexure is specifically designed to capture inventory flows within the commercial supply chain, again focusing on goods forming part of taxable supplies.

From a compliance perspective, the submission of either Annexure J or Annexure H-1 is now a mandatory component of the sales tax return, depending upon the nature of the business activity. It is important to note that both annexures are structured around the reporting of **taxable goods**, which remains the central qualifying criterion for disclosure. Accordingly, taxpayers must carefully assess the nature of their supplies to determine the applicability of the relevant annexure.

A critical practical implication arising from these changes is the requirement to accurately determine and document **closing stock as at December 31, 2024**, as this will form the opening stock for January 2025 under the revised reporting regime. Any inconsistency at this stage may lead to reconciliation issues in subsequent periods and could potentially trigger scrutiny from the tax authorities.

Overall, these amendments reflect FBR’s continued shift towards data-driven compliance and enhanced transparency across the supply chain. Taxpayers are therefore advised to align their internal systems, inventory records, and reporting mechanisms to ensure accurate and timely compliance with the revised requirements.
