Dear Sir,

We refer to your notice bearing reference No. UMS1040740466 regarding non-filing of Annexure H-1 for the last twelve tax periods, issued under Section 23 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 14 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 fileciteturn0file0L1-L8. At the outset, we sincerely thank your good office for granting an extension of time up to April 29, 2026.

At the very outset, it is respectfully submitted that Annexure H-1 is presently not enabled on the IRIS portal for our client, which itself makes compliance operationally unfeasible. Without prejudice to this limitation, we consider it important to clarify the substantive legal and practical position surrounding the applicability of Annexure H-1 vis-à-vis Annexure J.

Both Annexure H-1 and Annexure J fundamentally operate on the same underlying principle, i.e., reporting of stock and transaction-level details relating to **taxable supplies**. This position is evident from the structure of the Sales Tax Return and the prescribed annexures issued under the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 (including relevant SROs governing return formats and annexures), where the reporting framework is built around taxable activity forming part of the value chain. In other words, the starting point and core reporting requirement in both annexures is the disclosure of inventory and movements pertaining to taxable supplies.

In the present case, the primary business activity of our client does not involve taxable supplies in respect of the segment which appears to be the subject matter of your good office’s concern (i.e., fuel-related supplies), as such supplies are currently exempt from sales tax. Consequently, even if Annexure H-1 were to be enabled and filed, the very purpose intended—namely, capturing taxable supply chain data—would not be achieved, since the relevant transactions fall outside the ambit of taxable supplies. Therefore, the intended objective behind seeking Annexure H-1 data would remain unfulfilled in the facts and circumstances of our client’s case.

It is further submitted that our client is a manufacturing concern and is regularly filing Annexure J along with its sales tax returns, wherein complete and comprehensive details of inventory, consumption, and supplies relating to taxable operations are duly declared. The reporting under Annexure J adequately captures all relevant data required under the law, including any elements that may have a commercial or trading character.

We would also like to highlight, based on our practical experience and discussions held with your good office, that the system does not envisage simultaneous applicability of both Annexure H-1 and Annexure J. In fact, we are aware of instances within the oil marketing sector where, upon enabling Annexure H-1, Annexure J was automatically disabled at the system level. This clearly demonstrates that the framework is designed for alternate applicability depending upon the nature of business, and not cumulative compliance.

During our meeting with your good office, attended along with the client’s representative, these aspects were explained in detail, including the system constraints, nature of business, and the legal framework governing taxable versus exempt supplies. It was also clarified that the intention behind Annexure H-1—particularly in the context of fuel supply visibility—would not be practically served in cases where the underlying supplies are exempt.

In view of the above, it is respectfully submitted that there is no element of non-compliance on the part of our client. The non-filing of Annexure H-1 is attributable solely to its non-applicability and non-availability on the IRIS portal, while all required disclosures in respect of taxable activities are already being duly made through Annexure J in accordance with the prescribed law and procedure.

We trust the above adequately clarifies the position. However, should your good office require any further clarification or supporting documentation, we remain available at your convenience.

Yours faithfully,  
[Name]

Dear Sir,

We refer to your notice bearing reference No. UMS1040740466 regarding non-filing of Annexure H-1 for the last twelve tax periods, issued under Section 23 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 14 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 fileciteturn0file0L1-L8. At the outset, we sincerely thank your good office for granting an extension of time up to April 29, 2026.

At the very outset, it is respectfully submitted that Annexure H-1 is presently not enabled on the IRIS portal for our client, which itself makes compliance operationally impracticable. Without prejudice to this system limitation, we consider it important to clarify the legal position and the underlying framework introduced through S.R.O. 55(I)/2025 dated January 24, 2025, which governs the revised sales tax return and associated annexures.

Under the said S.R.O., the revised return format requires disclosure of **value and quantity of goods produced, acquired and supplied**, specifically in relation to **taxable goods**. In this context, Annexure J has been prescribed for manufacturers, whereas Annexure H-1 has been introduced for commercial importers, distributors and wholesalers. However, a careful reading of the prescribed formats and reporting fields clearly establishes that both annexures are fundamentally designed to capture **inventory movements and stock details relating to taxable supplies only**, with item-wise reporting based on HS Codes, units of measurement, and value/quantity reconciliation.

In the present case, the underlying business segment which appears to be the subject matter of the notice—i.e., fuel-related supplies—does not constitute taxable supplies, as petroleum products are currently operating under an **exempt regime** under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (as read with relevant exemption notifications/schedules). Accordingly, the very **starting point of reporting under both Annexure H-1 and Annexure J, i.e., taxable supplies, is not met** in respect of such transactions.

Therefore, even if Annexure H-1 were to be enabled for our client, the intended purpose behind its introduction—namely, capturing detailed quantitative data of taxable supply chains—would not be achieved in the facts of the present case. The disclosure mechanism under S.R.O. 55(I)/2025 is inherently linked to taxable goods, and cannot be meaningfully applied where the underlying supplies are exempt. This position aligns with the overall spirit and design of the revised return, which is to create a reconciliation framework for taxable inventory flows, rather than exempt supply chains.

It is further submitted that our client is a manufacturing concern and is duly complying with the requirement of filing Annexure J, wherein all relevant inventory and production details relating to its taxable operations are already being reported in accordance with the prescribed format. Any elements of procurement or supply that may carry a commercial character are also appropriately captured within the same annexure, ensuring full transparency and compliance with the law.

We would also like to respectfully highlight, based on practical system behavior and industry experience, that the IRIS system does not allow simultaneous applicability of Annexure J and Annexure H-1. We are aware of instances, including in the oil marketing sector, where upon enabling Annexure H-1, Annexure J was automatically disabled. This clearly indicates that the system—and by implication, the regulatory framework—envisages **mutually exclusive applicability** of these annexures depending on the nature of the taxpayer’s business, and not cumulative compliance.

These aspects were also explained during our meeting with your good office, attended along with the client’s representative, wherein we apprised you of the system limitations, the nature of supplies, and the scope of reporting under the revised return framework. It was also discussed that the rationale of seeking Annexure H-1 data for fuel supply visibility would not be fulfilled in cases where such supplies are exempt from sales tax.

In view of the above, it is respectfully submitted that there is no element of non-compliance on the part of our client. The non-filing of Annexure H-1 is attributable to (i) its non-availability on the IRIS portal, and (ii) its non-applicability in light of the nature of supplies and the legal framework governing taxable goods. All required disclosures relating to taxable activities are already being duly made through Annexure J, in line with S.R.O. 55(I)/2025 and the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

We trust the above clarifies the position. However, should your good office require any further clarification or supporting documentation, we remain available at your convenience.

Yours faithfully,  
[Name]

We refer to the clarification notice issued by your good office in respect of our application filed under section 151A read with section 159 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”), seeking issuance of exemption certificate in relation to withholding tax on gains arising from disposal of certain debt securities. We are grateful for the opportunity to clarify the legal position and respectfully submit the following for your kind consideration.

At the outset, it is most respectfully submitted that the reference made in the clarification notice to **Clause 99 of Part I of the Second Schedule** is not applicable to the facts of the present case. The said clause pertains to collective investment schemes and operates within a distinct legal framework, subject to specific distribution conditions. In contrast, the applicant fund is a **recognized provident fund**, whose income is categorically exempt under **Clause 57(3) of Part I of the Second Schedule** to the Ordinance. This exemption is unconditional in nature (subject to recognition status) and applies to the entirety of income derived by such fund. Accordingly, the taxability framework applicable to collective investment schemes under Clause 99 does not govern or restrict the position of a recognized provident fund.

Without prejudice to the above, it is further submitted that the observation made in the notice with reference to **Clause (47B) of Part IV of the Second Schedule**, to the effect that withholding provisions including section 151 may not apply, is respectfully incomplete in its application. While Clause (47B) does provide that certain withholding provisions shall not apply to specified persons, including recognized provident funds, the said clause does not in any manner curtail or override the independent statutory powers conferred upon the Commissioner under **section 159 of the Ordinance**.

In this regard, it is respectfully submitted that section 159 constitutes a self-contained procedural mechanism enabling the Commissioner to issue exemption certificates in cases where income is either wholly exempt or subject to reduced taxation. The existence of Clause (47B), which addresses non-applicability of withholding provisions in principle, does not negate the practical and procedural necessity of an exemption certificate. Rather, such certificate serves as a formal confirmation of the tax-exempt status to withholding agents, thereby ensuring correct application of law at the operational level.

This position finds strong support from the recent clarification issued by the Federal Board of Revenue dated March 27, 2026 in the context of mutual funds and pension schemes. While the said clarification refers to Clause 99 in the context of collective investment schemes, the underlying legal principle is of general application, namely that where income is exempt, the taxpayer is required to obtain an exemption certificate under section 159 for purposes of implementation. More importantly, industry representations acknowledged by the FBR clarify that even in situations covered under Clause (47B), exemption certificates continue to be issued as a matter of established practice to facilitate non-deduction of tax by withholding agents.

It is a well-settled principle of tax jurisprudence that withholding tax is merely a mechanism for collection of tax and cannot operate independently of the underlying tax liability. Where the income itself is exempt under the law, there exists no legal basis for deduction or collection of tax at source. However, in the absence of an exemption certificate, withholding agents—particularly financial institutions—continue to deduct tax as a matter of compliance prudence, resulting in avoidable cash flow constraints and accumulation of refundable tax balances. The issuance of exemption certificate, therefore, serves a critical administrative function in aligning practical compliance with the correct legal position.

In light of the above, it is respectfully submitted that:

- The applicant fund is governed by **Clause 57**, not Clause 99;  
- Its income is **fully exempt from tax**, and therefore not subject to withholding; and  
- The issuance of exemption certificate under **section 159 read with section 151A** is both legally permissible and practically necessary to ensure proper implementation of the law.

In view of the foregoing, we respectfully request your good office to kindly consider the above submissions and proceed with issuance of the exemption certificate for the relevant period. We remain available to provide any further clarification or documentation that may be required in this regard.

Yours faithfully,  
___

The exemption available under Clause 57 is distinct in nature and is not subject to the distribution-based conditions embedded in Clause 99. Accordingly, the legal framework governing collective investment schemes cannot be extended to or made applicable in the case of a recognized provident fund, and the reference to Clause 99 appears to be misplaced.

Without prejudice to the above, it is further submitted that the observation drawn from Clause (47B) of Part IV of the Second Schedule, regarding the non-applicability of withholding provisions including section 151, requires a more comprehensive appreciation. While the said clause provides for exclusion of certain withholding provisions in principle, it does not curtail or override the statutory authority vested in the Commissioner under section 159 of the Ordinance to issue exemption certificates. Section 159 operates as an independent procedural mechanism through which the exemption available under the law is given effect at the stage of withholding. The existence of a statutory exclusion and the issuance of an exemption certificate are therefore not mutually exclusive; rather, they operate in tandem to ensure that the legal position is properly implemented in practice.

In this context, it is pertinent to note that in the absence of an exemption certificate, withholding agents—particularly financial institutions—are generally constrained to adopt a conservative approach and proceed with deduction of tax, irrespective of the underlying exempt status of the recipient. This results in unnecessary withholding, leading to avoidable cash flow constraints and accumulation of refundable tax balances. The issuance of an exemption certificate under section 159 is thus essential from an administrative and compliance perspective, as it provides formal confirmation of the non-applicability of withholding provisions and ensures consistency in treatment by withholding agents.

This position also finds support from the recent clarification issued by the Federal Board of Revenue dated March 27, 2026 in relation to mutual funds and pension schemes, wherein it has been acknowledged that exemption from withholding is to be operationalized through the mechanism provided under section 159. While the said clarification refers to Clause 99 in the context of collective investment schemes, the principle underlying the same is of general application, namely that where income is exempt, the appropriate course is to obtain an exemption certificate to facilitate its practical implementation. Industry representations considered in that context further reinforce that even in cases where withholding provisions are stated to be non-applicable, exemption certificates continue to be issued as a matter of established practice to avoid ambiguity at the withholding stage.

It is also a settled principle of tax jurisprudence that withholding tax is merely a mode of collection and cannot operate independently of the underlying tax liability. Where income is wholly exempt under the law, there exists no legal basis for collection of tax at source. The exemption certificate, therefore, does not create the exemption; rather, it serves to operationalize and give effect to an exemption that already exists under the Ordinance.

In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the applicant’s case is governed by Clause 57(3) of Part I of the Second Schedule, under which its income is fully exempt from tax, and that the issuance of an exemption certificate under section 159 read with section 151A is both legally justified and administratively necessary. We therefore request your good office to kindly consider the submissions made herein and proceed with issuance of the exemption certificate for the relevant period. We remain available to provide any further clarification or supporting documentation that may be required in this regard.

Yours faithfully,  
___

Your query is valid and this is an area where practical interpretation matters, especially when determining **residential status under Section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**.

From a Pakistan tax perspective, the correct approach is to **count the number of days physically present in Pakistan** during the relevant tax year. The law clearly establishes residency based on presence in Pakistan (i.e., **183 days or more in a tax year**, or meeting the alternative 365-day test over two years). Therefore, the primary focus should always be on **Pakistan stay days**, not days spent abroad.

In terms of day-counting methodology, the generally accepted and defensible position (also followed in practice during assessments) is as follows:  
- **Days of presence in Pakistan are counted**, including partial days.  
- **Day of arrival in Pakistan is counted as a day in Pakistan.**  
- **Day of departure from Pakistan is typically not counted as a Pakistan day**, since the individual is considered to have left the country on that day.  

As a result, it is both **technically correct and practically advisable** to track and document **Pakistan stay days**, rather than trying to compute foreign stay days and derive Pakistan presence indirectly. This approach minimizes risk of mismatch during any future scrutiny by the tax authorities, particularly where immigration records are relied upon.

The advice you received is therefore aligned with best practice. For purposes of determining tax residency and avoiding any future disputes, you should **maintain a clear reconciliation of Pakistan stay days based on travel history (passport/immigration records)** and ensure that the 183-day threshold is assessed strictly on that basis.

The safest and most practical approach is:

- Stay **183 days in one country**, and  
- If possible, have some proof (like residency, visa, or tax record) from that country

Not all “183 days outside Pakistan” are equal.

You are broadly on the right track, but this area needs to be articulated very carefully because the law does **not operate exactly in the way it is commonly understood in practice**.

Under the Pakistan Income Tax framework, the primary test for an individual is contained in **section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, which simply looks at **presence in Pakistan**. If an individual is present in Pakistan for **183 days or more in a tax year (July to June)**, he is treated as a resident. Conversely, if Pakistan stay is below this threshold, the individual can fall into non-resident status—**irrespective of whether those days abroad are spent in one country or multiple countries**.

Now, coming to the point you have raised regarding the **“deeming provision” for Pakistani citizens**—this is where the nuance lies.

There *is* a specific deeming rule which essentially provides that a **citizen of Pakistan who is not present in any other country for 183 days or more in a tax year** may still be treated as a **resident of Pakistan**. The intent of this provision is to prevent situations where individuals artificially avoid residency by moving across multiple jurisdictions without establishing tax residency anywhere.

So practically, your interpretation aligns with how the law is *applied*, even if the wording is slightly different:

- If an individual spends **183+ days in one foreign country**, the position is clear—non-resident in Pakistan (subject to Pakistan stay being below threshold).
- If an individual **splits time across multiple countries**, and does not meet the **183-day threshold in any single country**, then:
  - For a **Pakistani citizen**, the risk arises that the tax authorities may invoke the deeming provision and treat the individual as **resident in Pakistan**.
  - This is particularly relevant where the person cannot demonstrate **tax residency elsewhere** (e.g., no tax residency certificate, no economic ties, etc.).

From a practical advisory perspective—which is what we typically recommend to clients—the safest and most defensible position is exactly what you have stated:

**Ensure 183 days in a single foreign jurisdiction**, and preferably obtain **tax residency evidence (TRC)** from that country.

This avoids:
- ambiguity under the deeming provision, and  
- unnecessary litigation or questioning by the tax authorities.

So in conclusion, while aggregation across multiple countries may technically satisfy “days outside Pakistan,” **it is not sufficient in isolation for Pakistani citizens**. To avoid being treated as a **tax resident of Pakistan**, you should be able to demonstrate tax residency in another country through a valid TRC for the relevant period. This is a very common point of confusion, so it’s important to separate two different concepts: **Pakistan tax residency** and **foreign tax residency**.

From a Pakistan tax perspective, the test is quite straightforward under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. An individual is treated as a **non-resident** if they spend **less than 183 days in Pakistan** during the tax year. The law does **not require** that the remaining days (i.e., days outside Pakistan) must be spent in a single foreign country.

Accordingly, if a person spends more than 183 days **outside Pakistan**, even across multiple countries (for example, UAE, Turkey, and the UK), they can still qualify as a **non-resident in Pakistan**, provided their physical presence in Pakistan remains below the 183-day threshold.

However, this is only one side of the picture. The practical issue arises on the **foreign side**. Most countries have their own tax residency rules (often also based on 183 days or other connection tests). If the individual does not meet the residency criteria of any one country, they may end up in a situation where:
- They are **non-resident in Pakistan**, and  
- Also **not considered a tax resident in any other country**

This is sometimes referred to as a “stateless tax position,” which can create complications such as:
- Difficulty in obtaining a **tax residency certificate (TRC)** from any jurisdiction  
- Challenges in availing **double tax treaty protections**  
- Increased scrutiny from tax authorities if income sources are unclear  

From a practical advisory standpoint, I generally recommend clients to **anchor their residency in at least one jurisdiction** (i.e., clearly meet the residency criteria of a specific country), rather than relying solely on being outside Pakistan for 183+ days across multiple locations.

So, in summary:  
Yes, for Pakistan purposes, days can be spread across multiple countries and you can still be non-resident. But from a broader tax planning and compliance perspective, it is always safer to establish clear residency in one jurisdiction to avoid future complications.

---

### **1. Super Tax Clarified: You Can’t Tax What Isn’t Taxable**

The Federal Constitutional Court has now settled a critical controversy — **Super Tax is not a standalone levy**, it is simply an *additional tax on income*. This means if a particular income stream is already exempt under the Income Tax Ordinance (for example, certain capital gains or agricultural income), then **Super Tax cannot be imposed on it**.

From a practical perspective, this is a major relief for taxpayers operating under exemptions or special regimes. Many businesses were facing aggressive positions from tax authorities where Super Tax was being applied even on exempt income. This ruling firmly establishes that **without a primary taxable base, no secondary tax can survive**, strengthening the legal position of taxpayers in ongoing disputes. fileciteturn0file0

---

### **2. Super Tax Disputes Deepen: Can FBR Charge Surcharge Without Allowing Adjustments?**

A serious legal contradiction has emerged. Courts have treated Super Tax under Section 4C as an **independent liability**, meaning taxpayers cannot adjust refunds or withholding taxes against it. However, at the same time, field formations are **imposing default surcharge and recovery proceedings**.

This creates a fundamental issue:

Best regards,

Below is a refined **combined appeal note** based on the attached grounds of appeal for **Securprint (Private) Limited — Tax Year 2026**, against the order dated March 30, 2026 passed under section 147 read with section 205 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. fileciteturn0file0

---

## Combined Appeal Note

The appellant respectfully submits that the impugned order bearing barcode No. 100000273983997 dated March 30, 2026, passed by the learned Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue under section 147 read with section 205 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, is without lawful authority, misconceived in law and liable to be annulled. The proceedings have been initiated and concluded on an erroneous assumption that section 147 permits the passing of an adjudicatory order for determination and enforcement of advance tax liability. This approach is contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance, as section 147 essentially provides for payment of advance tax during the tax year, which is provisional, adjustable and subject to final determination at the time of assessment or filing of return.

At the very outset, it is respectfully submitted that section 147 does not contemplate an assessment-like order for creation of a final demand. The liability under section 147 is not a final tax liability in itself; rather, it is an interim mechanism for collection of tax in advance, based on the prescribed statutory formula or on an estimate furnished by the taxpayer, as the case may be. Therefore, any demand created under section 147 must strictly remain within the limited scope of advance tax and cannot be converted into an enforceable assessed demand through an order which the law itself does not authorize.

The learned DCIR has erred in law by treating a provisional and adjustable advance tax amount as a final and recoverable demand. Reliance on section 147(7), if any, is legally misplaced. The said provision only enables recovery of unpaid advance tax after the relevant due date in the manner applicable to assessed tax; however, it does not confer jurisdiction upon the officer to pass an adjudicatory order determining liability in the nature of an assessment. A recovery mechanism cannot be enlarged into a charging or assessment provision. Accordingly, the impugned order suffers from inherent jurisdictional defect and is void ab initio.

Without prejudice to the above, the computation adopted by the learned DCIR is wholly arbitrary and unsupported by any disclosed basis. The impugned order does not identify whether the alleged advance tax liability has been computed with reference to the latest assessed income, the appellant’s current year estimate, any amended estimate, or any other legally recognized basis under section 147. No working, calculation sheet, reference to assessed income, tax already paid, tax credits, withholding taxes, brought forward adjustments or estimated current year liability has been provided. In absence of such basis, the demand is mechanical, non-speaking and legally unsustainable.

It is further submitted that the treatment of the amount of Rs. 23,704,758 is fundamentally erroneous. The impugned proceedings appear to have treated the entire amount, or substantially the entire amount, as default surcharge under section 205, without first lawfully establishing the principal liability under section 147. Section 205 is compensatory in nature and can only operate where there is a legally determined default in payment of tax. It cannot independently create a principal tax demand, nor can it substitute the advance tax liability itself. Therefore, unless the principal advance tax liability is properly computed and lawfully established, any levy of default surcharge is premature, arbitrary and without jurisdiction.

The default surcharge, if any, has also been imposed without providing the appellant with the basic particulars necessary to understand and contest the computation. The impugned order does not disclose the applicable rate, the precise period of alleged default, the due date considered by the officer, the amount on which surcharge has been computed, or the method used for calculation. Such non-disclosure violates the settled principles of transparency, due process and natural justice. A fiscal demand which is not supported by clear computation and reasons cannot be sustained merely because the department has described it as payable.

The subsequent recovery of the alleged amount through CPR No. IT-20260401-0101-1027757 dated April 01, 2026 is also illegal and without jurisdiction, as no valid and enforceable demand existed at the time of recovery. Section 137 deals with payment and recovery of tax payable pursuant to a valid order or legally enforceable demand. Where the foundational order itself is beyond the scope of section 147, any recovery based on such order automatically becomes unlawful. The recovery proceedings, including any coercive action or attachment of bank accounts, are therefore liable to be declared illegal and set aside.

It is also respectfully submitted that any coercive recovery action undertaken on the basis of the impugned order is contrary to law and due process. The department could not lawfully proceed to recover an amount which had neither been properly determined nor supported by a legally sustainable computation. Attachment of bank accounts or similar coercive measures, in such circumstances, amount to enforcement of an invalid demand and cause serious prejudice to the appellant’s business operations.

Without prejudice to the appellant’s primary position that the impugned order and recovery are unlawful, it is submitted in the alternative that the amount recovered through CPR No. IT-20260401-0101-1027757 dated April 01, 2026 has been incorrectly classified as “demanded income tax”. In substance, even on the department’s own assumption, the amount relates to advance tax under section 147. Since advance tax is adjustable against the final tax liability of the appellant for the relevant tax year, the classification of the payment as demanded income tax is incorrect and may adversely affect the appellant’s tax record and future adjustment position in IRIS.

In view of the above, it is respectfully prayed that the impugned order dated March 30, 2026 passed under section 147 read with section 205 of the Ordinance may kindly be annulled being without lawful authority and beyond the scope of law. It is further prayed that the recovery made through CPR No. IT-20260401-0101-1027757 dated April 01, 2026 may be declared illegal and without jurisdiction, and necessary directions may be issued for correction of the appellant’s tax record. Without prejudice, if the amount is not refunded, the learned officer may kindly be directed to reclassify the payment as advance tax under section 147 and allow proper adjustment thereof against the appellant’s final tax liability for Tax Year 2026.

The appellant craves leave to add, amend, alter, substitute or withdraw any ground or submission at or before the time of hearing.

## Combined Appeal Note  
**Securprint (Private) Limited — Tax Year 2026**  
**Appeal against Order under Section 147 read with Section 205 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**

The appellant respectfully submits that the impugned order bearing barcode No. 100000273983997 dated March 30, 2026, passed by the learned Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue under section 147 read with section 205 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, is without lawful authority, misconceived in law and liable to be annulled. The proceedings have been initiated and concluded on an erroneous assumption that section 147 permits the passing of an adjudicatory order for determination and enforcement of advance tax liability. This approach is contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance, as section 147 essentially provides for payment of advance tax during the tax year, which is provisional, adjustable and subject to final determination at the time of assessment or filing of return.

At the very outset, it is respectfully submitted that section 147 does not contemplate an assessment-like order for creation of a final demand. The liability under section 147 is not a final tax liability in itself; rather, it is an interim mechanism for collection of tax in advance, based on the prescribed statutory formula or on an estimate furnished by the taxpayer, as the case may be. Therefore, any demand created under section 147 must strictly remain within the limited scope of advance tax and cannot be converted into an enforceable assessed demand through an order which the law itself does not authorize.

The learned DCIR has erred in law by treating a provisional and adjustable advance tax amount as a final and recoverable demand. Reliance on section 147(7), if any, is legally misplaced. The said provision only enables recovery of unpaid advance tax after the relevant due date in the manner applicable to assessed tax; however, it does not confer jurisdiction upon the officer to pass an adjudicatory order determining liability in the nature of an assessment. A recovery mechanism cannot be enlarged into a charging or assessment provision. Accordingly, the impugned order suffers from inherent jurisdictional defect and is void ab initio.

Without prejudice to the above, the computation adopted by the learned DCIR is wholly arbitrary and unsupported by any disclosed basis. The impugned order does not identify whether the alleged advance tax liability has been computed with reference to the latest assessed income, the appellant’s current year estimate, any amended estimate, or any other legally recognized basis under section 147. No working, calculation sheet, reference to assessed income, tax already paid, tax credits, withholding taxes, brought forward adjustments or estimated current year liability has been provided. In absence of such basis, the demand is mechanical, non-speaking and legally unsustainable.

It is further submitted that the treatment of the amount of Rs. 23,704,758 is fundamentally erroneous. The impugned proceedings appear to have treated the entire amount, or substantially the entire amount, as default surcharge under section 205, without first lawfully establishing the principal liability under section 147. The invocation of section 205 is itself misconceived. Sub-section (1) of section 205, as drafted, does not extend to the present case in the manner assumed by the learned DCIR, as the legislature has separately provided specific conditions for levy of default surcharge in relation to advance tax under the relevant provisions of section 205. Therefore, section 205 cannot be invoked in a blanket manner merely by referring to section 147, particularly where the alleged principal liability itself has neither been lawfully determined nor finally crystallized.

The appellant’s case does not fall within the conditions contemplated under sub-section (3) of section 205. The said provision proceeds on the premise of a failure to pay tax or advance tax within the time required under the Ordinance. In the present case, however, no legally enforceable event of default had occurred when the impugned order was passed and the alleged recovery was made. The underlying proceedings and controversy regarding the alleged advance tax liability had not attained finality, and the appellant could not be treated as being in default before a valid and lawful determination of liability. In other words, the essential jurisdictional precondition for invoking default surcharge, namely an established failure to pay an amount lawfully due, was absent.

Similarly, sub-section (4) of section 205 applies in a different statutory situation and is linked with the prescribed threshold of payment of advance tax, including the requirement relating to payment of ninety percent of the tax chargeable. The said provision cannot be mechanically applied unless the department first establishes, on the basis of proper computation and legally admissible material, that the statutory threshold has in fact not been met. No such working has been provided in the impugned order. The learned DCIR has neither identified the correct tax chargeable nor compared the advance tax actually paid against the statutory ninety percent benchmark. In the absence of such computation, the invocation of section 205(4) is arbitrary, premature and legally unsustainable.

Section 205 is compensatory in nature and can only operate where there is a legally established default in payment of tax. It cannot independently create a principal tax demand, nor can it substitute the advance tax liability itself. Therefore, unless the principal advance tax liability is properly computed and lawfully established, and unless the conditions of the relevant sub-sections of section 205 are independently satisfied, any levy of default surcharge is premature, arbitrary and without jurisdiction. Accordingly, on a plain reading of section 205, the impugned levy of default surcharge is without lawful basis and liable to be deleted.

The default surcharge, if any, has also been imposed without providing the appellant with the basic particulars necessary to understand and contest the computation. The impugned order does not disclose the applicable rate, the precise period of alleged default, the due date considered by the officer, the amount on which surcharge has been computed, or the method used for calculation. Such non-disclosure violates the settled principles of transparency, due process and natural justice. A fiscal demand which is not supported by clear computation and reasons cannot be sustained merely because the department has described it as payable.

The subsequent recovery of the alleged amount through CPR No. IT-20260401-0101-1027757 dated April 01, 2026 is also illegal and without jurisdiction, as no valid and enforceable demand existed at the time of recovery. Section 137 deals with payment and recovery of tax payable pursuant to a valid order or legally enforceable demand. Where the foundational order itself is beyond the scope of section 147 and the levy under section 205 is without satisfaction of statutory preconditions, any recovery based on such order automatically becomes unlawful. The recovery proceedings, including any coercive action or attachment of bank accounts, are therefore liable to be declared illegal and set aside.

It is also respectfully submitted that any coercive recovery action undertaken on the basis of the impugned order is contrary to law and due process. The department could not lawfully proceed to recover an amount which had neither been properly determined nor supported by a legally sustainable computation. Attachment of bank accounts or similar coercive measures, in such circumstances, amount to enforcement of an invalid demand and cause serious prejudice to the appellant’s business operations.

Without prejudice to the appellant’s primary position that the impugned order and recovery are unlawful, it is submitted in the alternative that the amount recovered through CPR No. IT-20260401-0101-1027757 dated April 01, 2026 has been incorrectly classified as “demanded income tax”. In substance, even on the department’s own assumption, the amount relates to advance tax under section 147. Since advance tax is adjustable against the final tax liability of the appellant for the relevant tax year, the classification of the payment as demanded income tax is incorrect and may adversely affect the appellant’s tax record and future adjustment position in IRIS.

In view of the above, it is respectfully prayed that the impugned order dated March 30, 2026 passed under section 147 read with section 205 of the Ordinance may kindly be annulled being without lawful authority and beyond the scope of law. It is further prayed that the recovery made through CPR No. IT-20260401-0101-1027757 dated April 01, 2026 may be declared illegal and without jurisdiction, and necessary directions may be issued for correction of the appellant’s tax record. Without prejudice, if the amount is not refunded, the learned officer may kindly be directed to reclassify the payment as advance tax under section 147 and allow proper adjustment thereof against the appellant’s final tax liability for Tax Year 2026.

The appellant craves leave to add, amend, alter, substitute or withdraw any ground or submission at or before the time of hearing.

Below are refined social media posts based on the attached document. fileciteturn0file0

## 1. Tax Policy Must Support Growth, Not Punish Compliant Businesses

Pakistan’s tax policy is entering a very important phase where the real question is not only how much revenue the government collects, but how that revenue is collected. The Tax Policy Unit’s expected role in budget proposals for 2026-27 reflects a major shift towards rationalising taxes, supporting documented sectors, and restoring investor confidence. For too long, the formal and compliant businesses have remained the easiest target for additional taxation, while large portions of the informal economy continue to operate outside the tax net.

A sustainable tax system cannot be built by repeatedly increasing the burden on the same documented sectors. Multinational companies, large manufacturers, formal retailers, and regulated industries already contribute through income tax, sales tax, FED, withholding taxes, payroll taxes, and extensive compliance obligations. If tax policy continues to overburden these sectors, it may discourage new investment, reduce expansion, and push economic activity away from documentation.

The better approach is to broaden the tax base by gradually bringing undocumented retail, wholesale, small manufacturing, and informal supply chains into the system. Tax rationalisation should not be seen as a revenue loss; if designed properly, it can increase production, improve turnover, encourage investment, and ultimately generate higher overall tax collection from a wider and fairer base.

---

## 2. Over-Taxing Formal Sectors Can Shrink the Economy Instead of Growing Revenue

One of the strongest messages from the attached material is that Pakistan’s revenue strategy must move away from repeatedly taxing the already compliant sectors. Formal businesses operate transparently, maintain records, file returns, undergo audits, and remain visible to tax authorities. This visibility often makes them the first target whenever revenue pressure increases. However, this short-term approach creates long-term damage.

When documented sectors face frequent tax changes, higher FED, increased sales tax, and rising compliance costs, businesses become hesitant to invest. The exit or reduction of footprint by certain multinational companies also highlights how sensitive investors are to tax uncertainty and regulatory unpredictability. For any serious investor, tax policy consistency is as important as the tax rate itself.

Pakistan needs a tax framework where compliance is rewarded, not penalised. Rational tax rates, predictable policy, and fair enforcement across formal and informal markets can help rebuild business confidence. The real success of the Tax Policy Unit will depend on whether it can shift the focus from “collect more from the visible few” to “collect fairly from the wider economy.”

---

## 3. Milk Should Be Treated as Nutrition, Not a Luxury Product

The proposal to reduce sales tax on milk is not merely a tax relief measure; it is directly linked with food security, nutrition, affordability, and public health. In a country where malnutrition and child stunting remain serious concerns, milk cannot be treated like an ordinary taxable consumer product. High GST on processed milk increases prices, discourages formal processing, and keeps consumers dependent on loose milk markets where quality control is often weak.

The formal dairy sector already faces a major challenge because the majority of the milk economy remains informal. When high sales tax is imposed on processed milk, it makes safe and packaged milk less affordable for households, especially low- and middle-income families. This weakens the formal sector and reduces the incentive for investment in pasteurisation, testing, quality assurance, and safe milk supply chains.

A reduced GST rate, coupled with gradual documentation of the informal dairy market, can support both revenue and public welfare. The government should consider milk as a basic nutritional necessity. A balanced tax policy can make safe milk more affordable, encourage formalisation, support farmers, and improve public health outcomes at the same time.

---

## 4. Third Schedule Expansion Can Make Sales Tax Collection Simpler and More Transparent

The discussion around expanding the Third Schedule is highly relevant for Pakistan’s sales tax system. The current value-added model has been in place for many years, but gaps remain at different stages of the supply chain. In many cases, manufacturers end up absorbing additional taxes imposed on unregistered retailers because refusing supply may result in loss of shelf space. This creates unfair pressure on compliant businesses without necessarily documenting the retailer.

By collecting sales tax at the manufacturing stage on selected consumer goods, the Third Schedule can reduce leakages, simplify compliance, and improve price transparency for consumers. It also makes tax collection easier for the government because tax is captured at a visible and controlled point rather than chasing thousands of retailers operating outside the system.

Expansion of the Third Schedule to additional everyday consumer goods such as cooking oil, dairy products, frozen foods, flour, noodles, and other packaged items may help bring uniformity in collection. However, this policy must be implemented carefully so that it does not unnecessarily increase consumer prices. The objective should be fair tax collection, not additional inflation for households.

---

## 5. Early Market Closures Show That Tax Collection Depends on Economic Activity

The reported revenue loss due to early market closures highlights a very practical reality: tax collection cannot grow when business activity is slowing down. Reduced market timings, higher fuel prices, energy disruptions, and weaker consumer spending directly affect sales, income, turnover, and taxable transactions. When businesses sell less, the government also collects less.

This is why tax policy cannot be viewed in isolation. Revenue targets must be aligned with ground realities of the economy. If traders and industries are facing higher transportation costs, electricity issues, fuel price shocks, and reduced working hours, the tax machinery may struggle to meet targets even with higher tax rates.

The lesson is simple: a strong tax system needs a strong economy behind it. Instead of relying only on higher rates and indirect taxes, the government should focus on expanding the tax base, improving enforcement, stabilising energy supply, and supporting business continuity. More economic activity means more transactions, more documentation, and ultimately more sustainable revenue.

---

## 6. Reward Schemes for Tax Officers Must Be Transparent and Legally Defensible

The petition challenging FBR’s peer-ranking reward scheme raises an important question of public accountability. Any monetary reward paid from public funds must be backed by clear legal authority, transparent criteria, measurable performance standards, and proper oversight. Where rewards are distributed through internal mechanisms without sufficient transparency, concerns of favouritism, institutional bias, and misuse of public money naturally arise.

Tax officers play an important role in revenue enforcement, and performance incentives may have a valid place in tax administration. However, such incentives must not compromise fairness, independence, or taxpayer confidence. If reward structures are linked to aggressive tax demands or peer-based rankings without proper safeguards, they may create unhealthy pressure within the system.

A credible tax administration must be fair not only in collecting taxes but also in spending public money. Transparent reward rules, parliamentary oversight, audit mechanisms, and objective performance indicators are necessary to ensure that incentive schemes strengthen governance rather than create further controversy.

**Subject: Appeal Fixed for Hearing Before Tribunal – Input Tax Disallowance for July 2015 to June 2016**

Dear Haizan Sahib,

Hope you are doing well.

We would like to inform you that the appeal in your case has been fixed for hearing tomorrow before the Tribunal. By way of background, the matter relates to disallowance of input tax amounting to approximately Rs. 92 million for the tax period from July 2015 to June 2016.

This is the second round of appeal proceedings. In the first round, the officer had disallowed the input tax through a show cause notice without providing invoice-wise details of the alleged inadmissible input tax. At that stage, we had specifically requested the officer to provide the invoice-wise working/listing so that the matter could be properly reconciled and responded to. However, the required details were not provided, and the order was passed. We thereafter filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), who accepted our contention and remanded the matter back to the officer with the direction to provide proper opportunity and share the relevant invoice-wise details.

During the remand proceedings, we again reiterated the same position and requested the officer to provide the specific invoice-wise details forming the basis of the proposed disallowance. However, the officer again proceeded to pass the order on more or less similar lines, taking the position that the relevant figures had been extracted from the taxpayer’s own declarations and, therefore, the details should already be readily available with the taxpayer.

In this regard, we had also discussed the matter with you earlier. As per your understanding, the input tax actually claimed from the suppliers/parties referred to in the order during the relevant tax period appears to be higher than the amount confronted by the officer. Accordingly, in the absence of invoice-wise particulars, it is not possible to identify which specific input tax invoices are being alleged as inadmissible and which invoices are not being disputed. Due to this lack of specific information, we are unable to prepare a complete and effective reconciliation or offer a proper factual response to the allegation.

Having said that, on review of the notice/order, it appears that the input tax referred to by the officer largely relates to suppliers connected with steel, construction, fixtures and fittings, and similar items. To that extent, there is a foreseeable factual and legal exposure, as the department may argue that such input tax relates to activities or assets not directly forming part of taxable activity. Further, there are certain adverse decisions available up to the High Court level on input tax relating to construction, civil works and similar capital items. Therefore, while our primary ground remains that invoice-wise details were not provided despite repeated requests, we also need to be fully prepared on the factual nature of the parties and the underlying input tax.

In view of the above, kindly confirm at your earliest whether our understanding is correct that the party-wise input tax appearing in the order is lower than the input tax actually claimed from the same suppliers during the relevant period. This confirmation will help us take the position before the Tribunal that the department has failed to identify the specific disputed invoices and that, without such invoice-wise details, the disallowance cannot be properly verified or responded to.

For your reference, we are enclosing herewith a copy of the original assessment order passed in the first round of proceedings. Since the appeal is fixed for hearing tomorrow before the Tribunal, we would appreciate your urgent response on the above.  

Best regards,  
[Your Name]
